tamil:
சிற்றினம் அஞ்சும் பெருமை சிறுமைதான்
சுற்றமாச் சூழ்ந்து விடும்.
transliteration:
Sitrinam anjum perumai sirumaidhaan
Sutramaach soozhndhu vidum.
current_meaning: Greatness fears the company of the mean-minded, but smallness embraces such people and gathers them round as its own kin.
elementary_explanation: A truly great person is careful to stay away from petty, mean-spirited people, almost as if afraid of them. A small-minded person does the opposite: they happily pull those same people close and treat them like family.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter by defining two temperaments through a single reaction: அஞ்சும் (‘fears, shrinks from’) versus சுற்றமாச் சூழ்ந்து விடும் (‘surrounds itself with them as kinsfolk’). The சிற்றினம் (‘small/mean kind’) are not necessarily criminals; commentators such as Parimelazhagar gloss them as the base-minded whose company slowly lowers one’s own standard. The chiasmus of பெருமை/சிறுமை (greatness/smallness) makes character a matter of affinity: we show what we are by whom we are comfortable with. This chapter is the deliberate counterweight to chapter 45 (பெரியாரைத் துணைக்கோடல, seeking the help of the great): what one should seek there, one should fear here.

tamil:
நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர்திரிந் தற்றாகும் மாந்தர்க்கு
இனத்தியல்ப தாகும் அறிவு.
transliteration:
Nilaththiyalbaal neerthirindhu atraakum maandharkku
Inaththiyalba thaagum arivu.
current_meaning: Just as water changes its nature according to the soil it flows through, a person’s understanding takes on the nature of the company they keep.
elementary_explanation: Rain is pure when it falls, but it turns muddy, salty or sweet depending on the ground it runs over. Our minds work the same way: they pick up the colour and taste of the people we spend time with.
university_explanation: The simile works because rain is pure when it falls and only takes on colour, salt or sweetness from the ground (நிலத்தியல்பு) it touches. அறிவு here is not raw intelligence but practical understanding, the judgement a person brings to life. Valluvar’s claim is environmental: the mind is not a sealed container but something that absorbs from its surroundings. The next two couplets (453–454) sharpen this into a paradox: intelligence seems to belong to the mind but is actually supplied by one’s company.

tamil:
மனத்தானாம் மாந்தர்க் குணர்ச்சி இனத்தானாம்
இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல்.
transliteration:
Manaththaanaam maandhark kunarchchi inaththaanaam
Innaan enappadunj chol.
current_meaning: A person’s perception comes from their own mind, but the verdict “he is such-and-such a man” comes from the company they keep.
elementary_explanation: What you think and feel comes from inside you. But what other people say about you, like ‘he’s a good guy’ or ‘he’s trouble’, mostly depends on who your friends are.
university_explanation: The couplet sets inner and outer against each other: உணர்ச்சி (perception, awareness) arises from மனம் (mind), while reputation, இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல் (‘the word by which one is called such a man’), arises from இனம் (one’s group). This is a sociological observation: others cannot see into a person’s mind, so they judge by association. Valluvar does not call this judgement unfair. He treats it as a fact the prudent must reckon with, which is why the chapter sits in the Porul (polity) book rather than Aram. Together with 454 it forms a two-step argument: first reputation, then even inner wisdom, turns out to depend on one’s company.

tamil:
மனத்து ளதுபோலக் காட்டி ஒருவற்கு
இனத்துள தாகும் அறிவு.
transliteration:
Manaththu ladhupolak kaatti oruvarku
Inaththu ladhaagum arivu.
current_meaning: Wisdom appears to belong to a person’s own mind, but it really resides in the company they keep.
elementary_explanation: We think our good sense is all our own. But look closely and much of it comes from the people around us: what they talk about, what they value, how they act.
university_explanation: காட்டி (‘making it appear’) is the key word. Valluvar grants that wisdom seems to live in one’s own mind, then corrects the appearance: it is actually இனத்துளது, lodged in one’s group. This is a strikingly early statement of what is now called distributed or socially embedded cognition: judgement is sustained by the conversations, norms and examples of a circle. It does not deny individual minds, which 453 affirmed, but it undercuts the pride of thinking oneself self-sufficient. The practical corollary, drawn out in 455–460, is that choosing one’s company is choosing one’s wisdom.

tamil:
மனந்தூய்மை செய்வினை தூய்மை இரண்டும்
இனந்தூய்மை தூவா வரும்.
transliteration:
Mananthooimai seivinai thooimai irandum
Inanthooimai thoovaa varum.
current_meaning: Purity of mind and purity of deeds both come about through the purity of one’s company.
elementary_explanation: Having a clean heart and doing clean, honest things are both easier when the people around you are good. Good friends act like a support that keeps your thoughts and actions straight.
university_explanation: தூவா (‘support, prop, means’) is the pivot. Purity of mind (மனம்) and of action (செய்வினை), the two pillars of Aram, are made to depend on a third thing, purity of company (இனம்). This goes a step beyond 452’s simile: company is not just an influence on character but its enabling support. The triple repetition of தூய்மை holds the three purities together in one sound-chain, mirroring the argument. Parimelazhagar notes that although mind and deed seem to be individual possessions, they are sustained by one’s associates.

tamil:
மனந்தூயார்க் கெச்சம்நன் றாகும் இனந்தூயார்க்
கில்லைநன் றாகா வினை.
transliteration:
Mananthooyaark kechcham nanraagum inanthooyaark
Killai nanraakaa vinai.
current_meaning: The pure-minded leave behind a good legacy, and those whose company is pure do no deed that is not good.
elementary_explanation: People with clean hearts leave good things behind them: good children, a good name. People whose friends are good never end up doing bad things, because their friends keep them on track.
university_explanation: எச்சம் (‘that which remains’) is read by Parimelazhagar as good progeny, and by others as the good name that outlives a person; both senses make purity of mind a matter of legacy. The second line is sharper: for those with pure company there is no deed that is not good (இல்லை நன்றாகா வினை). The double negative is emphatic. Good company does not merely encourage good action; it rules out bad action. The couplet divides the labour: the mind decides what one leaves behind, and company decides what one does.

tamil:
மனநலம் மன்னுயிர்க் காக்கம் இனநலம்
எல்லாப் புகழுந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Mananalam mannuyirk kaakkam inanalam
Ellaap pugazhum tharum.
current_meaning: Goodness of mind brings prosperity to a person, and goodness of company brings every kind of renown.
elementary_explanation: A good heart helps you do well in life. But good friends give you something extra: they help people everywhere know and respect you.
university_explanation: Here the parallelism moves from purity (தூய்மை) to goodness (நலம்), and the rewards from legacy to worldly outcomes: ஆக்கம் (prosperity, growth) from the mind, எல்லாப் புகழும் (every kind of fame) from company. The word எல்லா (‘all’) quietly ranks the second above the first. Prosperity may be private, but fame is by nature social and so depends on one’s circle. The couplet explains why reputation, discussed in 453, is not just vanity: in the Porul context of kingship and public life, renown is a resource, and it flows through association.

tamil:
மனநலம் நன்குடைய ராயினும் சான்றோர்க்கு
இனநலம் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Mananalam nankudaiya raayinum saanrorkku
Inanalam emaap pudaiththu.
current_meaning: Even for the wise, who already have fine goodness of mind, good company is a source of security and strength.
elementary_explanation: Even very good and wise people still need good friends. Good company works like a protective wall that keeps their goodness safe.
university_explanation: The concessive ஆயினும் (‘even though’) blocks the obvious objection: surely the already-good (சான்றோர்) do not need company? Valluvar replies that for them too, இனநலம் is ஏமாப்பு, security or fortification. The word suggests protection against the slow wearing-down of virtue by circumstance. Virtue, on this view, is not a fixed possession but a condition to be kept up, and company is part of the upkeep. The couplet guards against the moral self-sufficiency that 454 already undercut.

tamil:
மனநலத்தின் ஆகும் மறுமைமற் றஃதும்
இனநலத்தின் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
transliteration:
Mananalaththin aakum marumaimat rahdhum
Inanalaththin emaap pudaiththu.
current_meaning: Bliss in the world to come is gained through goodness of mind, and even that is made secure by goodness of company.
elementary_explanation: A good heart earns you happiness after this life. But good friends make that happiness even more certain by helping you stay good all the way through.
university_explanation: The previous couplet made good company a fortress for virtue in this life; this one extends the claim to மறுமை, the next world. Even the reward that seems most purely individual, earned by one’s own inner goodness (மனநலம்), is secured (ஏமாப்பு, repeated from 458) by one’s company. The மற்று… அஃதும் (‘and even that’) is emphatic. The pairing of 458 and 459 moves from this world to the next and leaves no domain where company does not matter.

tamil:
நல்லினத்தி னூங்குந் துணையில்லை தீயினத்தின்
அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்.
transliteration:
Nallinaththin oongum thunaiyillai theeyinaththin
Allar paduppadhooum il.
current_meaning: There is no greater help than good company, and nothing causes more affliction than bad company.
elementary_explanation: Good friends are the best help you can ever have. Bad friends are the worst trouble you can ever have. Nothing else comes close in either direction.
university_explanation: The chapter ends with a symmetrical superlative: nothing surpasses (ஊங்கு) good company as a support (துணை), and nothing causes as much suffering (அல்லல்) as bad company. The emphatic lengthening in படுப்பதூஉம் (an alapedai, or metrical vowel extension) stresses the second half, so the warning weighs more than the praise, in keeping with the chapter title. The couplet sums up the whole adhikaram and connects it to chapter 45: seek the great, avoid the small, because nothing else in life has as much power to help or harm.

tamil:
அழிவதூஉம் ஆவதூஉம் ஆகி வழிபயக்கும்
ஊதியமும் சூழ்ந்து செயல்.
transliteration:
Azhivadhooum aavadhooum aaki vazhipayakkum,
Oodhiyamum soozhndhu seyal.
current_meaning: Before you act, weigh what will be lost, what will be gained, and the net benefit that will follow afterwards; only then undertake the action.
elementary_explanation: Before you start something, ask three questions: What might I lose? What will I get? And after everything is added up, will it really be worth it? Only when you have thought about all three should you begin.
university_explanation: The opening couplet sets out a three-part calculus that governs the whole chapter: அழிவது (what is spent or destroyed at the outset — the cost), ஆவது (what comes into being — the gain), and வழிபயக்கும் ஊதியம் (the profit that results in due course — the net yield after costs are subtracted). The verb சூழ் (to deliberate, to survey all round) is the chapter’s keyword. Parimelazhagar reads the triad as capital outlay, return, and eventual surplus, which makes this one of the earliest cost-benefit formulations in world ethical literature. Placed in the Porul (polity) section, the kural is addressed first to rulers, but it is phrased generally enough to apply to any undertaking. The point is not to avoid risk but to see the whole ledger before committing.

tamil:
தெரிந்த இனத்தொடு தேர்ந்தெண்ணிச் செய்வார்க்கு
அரும்பொருள் யாதொன்றும் இல்.
transliteration:
Therindha inaththotu therndhennich cheyvaarkku,
Arumporul yaadhondrum il.
current_meaning: For those who act after deliberating carefully with well-chosen counsellors, and after examining the matter themselves, nothing is too difficult to achieve.
elementary_explanation: If you pick good, trustworthy friends, talk your plan over with them, and think it through yourself too, there is almost nothing you cannot get done.
university_explanation: The couplet joins two acts of discernment: தெரிந்த இனம் (a circle that has itself been tested and chosen — echoing the preceding chapters on seeking the help of the great and avoiding mean company, 44–46) and தேர்ந்து எண்ணி (having examined and reasoned). Counsel is only as good as the counsellors, so selection comes before consultation. The strong universal claim (‘no object is hard to attain’) is typical of Valluvar’s rhetoric, which states the ideal case to motivate the practice. The idea of the ruler’s council (mantra) was a central institution of classical Indian statecraft, and the Kural places it at the heart of deliberate action.

tamil:
ஆக்கம் கருதி முதலிழக்கும் செய்வினை
ஊக்கார் அறிவுடை யார்.
transliteration:
Aakkam karudhi mudhalizhakkum seyvinai,
Ookkaar arivutai yaar.
current_meaning: The wise will not attempt an undertaking that, in the hope of future profit, risks losing the capital they already have.
elementary_explanation: Smart people don’t risk everything they already have just because they hope to win something bigger. They protect what they have first.
university_explanation: The pairing ஆக்கம் (gain, increase) and முதல் (principal, capital) is commercial vocabulary and continues the ledger of 461. The verb ஊக்கார் (‘they will not be eager to / will not set about’) matters: Valluvar does not ban all risk, but says the wise will not be enthusiastic for ventures where the principal itself is at stake. This is a rule of prudence rather than timidity. It tells a ruler not to gamble the treasury or the kingdom’s security on speculative expansion. Later chapters praise energy and persistence (ஊக்கம், chapter 60), so the teaching is best read as ‘secure the base before seeking growth’.

tamil:
தெளிவி லதனைத் தொடங்கார் இளிவென்னும்
ஏதப்பாடு அஞ்சு பவர்.
transliteration:
Thelivi ladhanaith thotangaar ilivennum,
Edhappaatu anju bavar.
current_meaning: Those who fear the disgrace of failure will not begin any undertaking whose outcome and means are not clear to them.
elementary_explanation: People who care about their good name don’t start things they don’t fully understand, because failing halfway would make them look foolish.
university_explanation: தெளிவு (clarity, certainty) is the key concept: an undertaking is ‘தெளிவு இலது’ when its means, outcome, or one’s own ability to finish it are uncertain. The motive for restraint is இளிவு (humiliation, contempt), described as an ஏதப்பாடு (a harm or calamity). Valluvar treats reputation as a real asset of the ruler, and public failure as damage to it, not just wounded pride. Commentators differ slightly. Parimelazhagar stresses that the doubtful venture ends in ridicule, while modern commentators such as Kalaignar read it more broadly as avoiding dishonourable acts. Both readings rest on the same logic: foreseeable shame is itself a cost to include in deliberation.

tamil:
வகையறச் சூழா தெழுதல் பகைவரைப்
பாத்திப் படுப்பதோ ராறு.
transliteration:
Vakaiyarach choozhaa thezhudhal pakaivaraip,
Paaththip patuppadho raaru.
current_meaning: To rise against enemies without thoroughly planning every aspect of the campaign is a way of planting them in a prepared bed where they will grow strong.
elementary_explanation: If you rush to fight someone without planning properly, you actually help them — like planting a seed in good soil and watering it so it grows bigger.
university_explanation: The metaphor is agricultural. பாத்தி is a prepared garden bed, and பாத்திப் படுத்தல் means settling a plant in such a bed so it takes root. A poorly planned attack does not just fail. It strengthens the enemy, who gains confidence, allies, and legitimacy from beating back a rash assault. வகையற (exhaustively, covering every category) points to the sixfold considerations of statecraft (strength, place, time, means, allies, and so on) that commentators read into the phrase. Pope renders it: ‘With plans not well matured to rise against your foe, / Is way to plant him out where he is sure to grow!’ It is the chapter’s one explicitly military couplet.

tamil:
செய்தக்க அல்ல செயக்கெடும் செய்தக்க
செய்யாமை யானுங் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Seydhakka alla seyak ketum seydhakka,
Seyyaamai yaanung ketum.
current_meaning: One is ruined by doing what ought not to be done, and one is equally ruined by failing to do what ought to be done.
elementary_explanation: You can get into trouble in two ways: by doing something you shouldn’t, and by not doing something you should. Both can hurt you just as much.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a chiastic repetition of செய்தக்க (‘what is fit to be done’). It balances sins of commission against sins of omission and treats both as equally ruinous (கெடும் … கெடும்). This keeps the chapter from turning into a counsel of timidity: deliberation is meant to discern the right action, and paralysis is as fatal as rashness. In a political reading, a ruler who neglects necessary measures (defence, justice, relief) falls as surely as one who pursues reckless ones. The same double structure is familiar from moral and legal traditions that separate positive duties from prohibitions.

tamil:
எண்ணித் துணிக கருமம் துணிந்தபின்
எண்ணுவம் என்பது இழுக்கு.
transliteration:
Ennith thunika karumam thunindhapin,
Ennuvam enbadhu izhukku.
current_meaning: Think carefully, then resolve upon a course of action; to say ‘we will think about it after we have begun’ is a disgrace.
elementary_explanation: Do your thinking first, then make up your mind and go. Starting first and figuring it out later is a big mistake.
university_explanation: Probably the most-quoted couplet of the chapter. Its force comes from the sequence எண்ணி → துணிக (reflect → resolve) and the rejection of the reversed order துணிந்தபின் எண்ணுவம் (‘having resolved, we shall reflect’). Two faults are excluded at once. One is beginning without deliberation. The other, implied, is wavering and reopening the question after committing, which dissipates resolve. துணிவு means both decision and courage, so the couplet unites prudence and boldness: deliberation belongs before action, and firmness belongs after decision. இழுக்கு (a slip, a blemish) casts the failure as a lapse of character, not merely of technique.

tamil:
ஆற்றின் வருந்தா வருத்தம் பலர்நின்று
போற்றினும் பொத்துப் படும்.
transliteration:
Aatrin varundhaa varuththam palarnindru,
Potrinum poththup patum.
current_meaning: Effort not spent in the proper way will fail, even if many people stand by to support and protect the work.
elementary_explanation: If you work hard but in the wrong way, the project will fall apart — even if lots of people are trying to help hold it together.
university_explanation: ஆறு here means ‘way, proper method’. வருந்தா வருத்தம் (‘toil not toiled [in the right way]’) is effort poured out without a method. The verb போற்று (to guard, cherish, maintain) and பலர்நின்று (many standing together) anticipate the objection that sheer numbers or goodwill can make up for bad method. Valluvar denies it. பொத்துப் படும் means ‘it will spring a leak / be breached’, an image of a vessel or dam giving way. The couplet adds to the chapter’s argument: deliberation must choose not only whether to act but how, and a wrong method cannot be rescued by resources applied afterwards.

tamil:
நன்றாற்ற லுள்ளுந் தவறுண்டு அவரவர்
பண்பறிந் தாற்றாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Nandraatra lullun thavaruntu avaravar,
Panbarin dhaatraak katai.
current_meaning: Even in doing good there can be failure, if one acts without understanding the particular nature of each person concerned.
elementary_explanation: Even being kind can go wrong if you don’t understand the person you’re helping. What helps one person might upset another.
university_explanation: The couplet carries deliberation into benevolence itself. நன்று ஆற்றல் (doing good, conferring benefits) is normally praised without qualification, but Valluvar notes a தவறு (error, failure) that arises when one does not know அவரவர் பண்பு (the respective natures of each person). Parimelazhagar explains that benefits given to those whose nature does not suit them may be misused or may turn them hostile. For a ruler, rewards and favours are tools of policy and must fit their recipients. The reduplicated அவரவர் (‘each respectively’) insists on individual discernment rather than uniform treatment. Some editions spell the verb தவுறுண்டு; the standard reading is தவறுண்டு.

tamil:
எள்ளாத எண்ணிச் செயல்வேண்டும் தம்மொடு
கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது உலகு.
transliteration:
Ellaadha ennich cheyalventum thammotu,
Kollaadha kollaadhu ulagu.
current_meaning: One should think carefully and do only what will not bring the world’s scorn; for the world will not approve of what does not befit one’s own position and character.
elementary_explanation: Before you act, ask: will good people respect this, and does it fit who I am? People won’t accept actions that don’t suit the person doing them.
university_explanation: The closing couplet adds a social test to the practical tests of the preceding kurals. எள்ளாத (‘what is not despised’) introduces public judgement, and the wordplay கொள்ளாத கொள்ளாது (‘the world will not accept what is not accepted with oneself’) sets the criterion of fit. An action must suit the agent’s station, capacity and character (தம்மொடு). Parimelazhagar takes it that the world will not approve deeds out of keeping with one’s status, even when the deeds themselves are not bad. For a ruler, legitimacy depends on acting in ways subjects and peers can recognise as fitting. The chapter thus ends by setting individual calculation inside a community of judgement.

tamil:
வினைவலியும் தன்வலியும் மாற்றான் வலியும்
துணைவலியும் தூக்கிச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Vinaivaliyum thanvaliyum maatraan valiyum
Thunaivaliyum thookkich cheyal.
current_meaning: Before acting, weigh four strengths against one another: the strength the task demands, your own strength, your opponent’s strength, and the strength of the allies who will stand with each side.
elementary_explanation: Before you start something big, stop and measure four things: how hard the job is, how strong you are, how strong the other side is, and who will help each of you. Only after weighing all four should you decide to go ahead.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter with a four-part audit: vinai-vali (the strength the undertaking requires), tan-vali (one’s own strength), maatraan-vali (the adversary’s) and thunai-vali (the strength of allies, which Parimelazhagar reads as the allies of both parties). The verb thookki, ‘weighing as on a balance’, governs all four terms, so action (seyal) is justified only by comparison. Assessing yourself alone is not enough. This is the centre of the Kural’s political realism, and it closely parallels Kautilya’s Arthaśāstra, whose ninth book opens with a chapter on knowing power, place, time, strength and weakness before any campaign. Prudence here is not timidity. It is what makes effective action possible.

tamil:
ஒல்வ தறிவது அறிந்ததன் கண்தங்கிச்
செல்வார்க்குச் செல்லாதது இல்.
transliteration:
Olvadhu arivadhu arindhadhan kan thangich
Chelvaarkkuch chellaadhadhu il.
current_meaning: Nothing is out of reach for those who know what they can do, learn what the task requires, and then keep steadily at it as they go forward.
elementary_explanation: If you know what you’re able to do, learn everything you need for it, and then stick with it without giving up, there’s nothing you can’t reach.
university_explanation: This couplet turns the caution of 471 into confidence. It has three stages: olvadhu (discerning what is within one’s power), arivadhu (acquiring the knowledge the task needs) and thangi (settling into the work with steady application). The conclusion, chellaadhadhu il (‘there is nothing that will not go’ for such people), is not a claim to unlimited power. It is conditional: success without limit is promised only inside the field that honest self-assessment has marked out. Knowing your limits is exactly what lets you be effective within them. The verse also defends Valluvar’s realism against the charge of defeatism, since measuring your strength is meant to lead to action, not to paralysis.

tamil:
உடைத்தம் வலியறியார் ஊக்கத்தின் ஊக்கி
இடைக்கண் முரிந்தார் பலர்.
transliteration:
Udaiththam valiyariyaar ookkaththin ookki
Idaikkan murindhaar palar.
current_meaning: Many who did not know the true measure of their own strength, and plunged into an undertaking on enthusiasm alone, have broken down midway.
elementary_explanation: Lots of people get very excited and jump into something big without checking whether they’re strong enough. Halfway through they run out of strength, and it all falls apart.
university_explanation: Udaiththam vali, ‘the strength they themselves possess’, is exactly what these people fail to know. Ookkam (zeal, drive) is praised elsewhere in the Kural, with a whole chapter on it (ch. 60, Ookkam Udaimai), so Valluvar is not condemning enthusiasm itself. He condemns enthusiasm cut loose from measurement. The verb murindhaar (‘they snapped’) suggests a branch or axle giving way under strain and looks ahead to the cart-axle image of 475. Palar (‘many’) gives the verse an empirical, historical tone: this is not a hypothetical but a pattern seen across many careers and kingdoms.

tamil:
அமைந்தாங் கொழுகான் அளவறியான் தன்னை
வியந்தான் விரைந்து கெடும்.
transliteration:
Amaindhaangu ozhugaan alavariyaan thannai
Viyandhaan viraindhu kedum.
current_meaning: One who does not act in harmony with others, does not know the measure of his own strength, and admires himself, will quickly come to ruin.
elementary_explanation: Someone who won’t get along with others, doesn’t know how strong they really are, and keeps bragging about how great they are will fall very fast.
university_explanation: Three faults are linked here. The first is failing to fit one’s conduct to others (amaindhaangu ozhugaan, which commentators read as refusing to accommodate those around one, especially more powerful neighbours). The second is ignorance of one’s own measure (alavu ariyaan). The third is self-admiration (thannai viyandhaan). The first two are errors of judgement, and the third is the emotional state that keeps them going, because the self-admirer stops checking. Viraindhu (‘swiftly’) matters: pride does not merely lead to ruin eventually, it speeds it up.

tamil:
பீலிபெய் சாகாடும் அச்சிறும் அப்பண்டஞ்
சால மிகுத்துப் பெயின்.
transliteration:
Peelipey saakaadum achchirum appandanj
Chaala miguththup peyin.
current_meaning: Even a cart loaded with peacock feathers will have its axle break if the load is piled on beyond measure.
elementary_explanation: A peacock feather weighs almost nothing. But if you pile far too many onto a cart, even feathers will snap its axle. Lots of small things can add up to too much.
university_explanation: This is one of the Kural’s most famous images. The peacock feather (peeli) is the lightest of loads and the cart (saakaadu) a sturdy vehicle, yet when it is loaded chaala miguththu (‘in great excess’), the axle (achchu) breaks. Parimelazhagar applies the verse to kings: even weak enemies can overwhelm a strong ruler if they combine, so a king should not provoke many small foes at once. A broader reading applies it to any capacity. No strength is infinite, and sheer quantity can turn trifles into a fatal burden. The image anticipates the later proverb of the straw that breaks the camel’s back.

tamil:
நுனிக்கொம்பர் ஏறினார் அஃதிறந் தூக்கின்
உயிர்க்கிறுதி ஆகி விடும்.
transliteration:
Nunikkombar erinaar ahdhirandhu ookkin
Uyirkkirudhi aagi vidum.
current_meaning: Those who have climbed to the very tip of a branch will lose their lives if they try to climb beyond it.
elementary_explanation: Imagine climbing a tree right out to the thinnest tip of a branch. If you try to go even further, the branch breaks and you fall. You need to know when you’ve gone as high as you safely can.
university_explanation: Nunikkombar, the thin end of a branch, marks the exact limit of what one’s strength, and the support one relies on, can bear. Commentators apply it to a ruler who has already stretched his power as far as it will go: any further push (ahdhu irandhu ookkin, ‘if he strives beyond it’) becomes fatal. The verse pairs with 475. There an external load exceeds capacity; here one’s own ambition exceeds the support beneath. The image is precise: the danger is greatest exactly when one is highest.

tamil:
ஆற்றின் அளவறிந்து ஈக அதுபொருள்
போற்றி வழங்கு நெறி.
transliteration:
Aatrin alavarindhu eega adhuporul
Potri vazhangu neri.
current_meaning: Give in the right way, knowing the measure of your means. That is the way to preserve your wealth while still giving it.
elementary_explanation: Being generous is good, but give in a way that fits what you actually have. That way you can keep helping people and still keep your household going.
university_explanation: Here the chapter turns from military to economic power, since for Valluvar wealth is also a form of vali. Aatrin means ‘in the proper way’, or in some readings ‘according to one’s capacity’. Alavu arindhu means knowing the measure of one’s wealth. The couplet reconciles two duties that could conflict: potri (preserving) and vazhangu (distributing). Measured giving is not stinginess. It is the method (neri) that makes generosity sustainable. Some web editions print aravarindhu here, but the standard Parimelazhagar text and most editions read alavarindhu, ‘knowing the measure’, which fits the chapter’s theme.

tamil:
ஆகாறு அளவிட்டி தாயினுங் கேடில்லை
போகாறு அகலாக் கடை.
transliteration:
Aagaaru alavittidhu aayinum kedillai
Pogaaru agalaak kadai.
current_meaning: Even if the channel through which income flows in is narrow, there is no harm, as long as the channel through which it flows out is not wider.
elementary_explanation: It’s OK if you don’t earn much. What matters is that you don’t spend more than you earn. A small income with even smaller spending keeps you safe.
university_explanation: Aagaaru (the way wealth comes in) and pogaaru (the way it goes out) are channel metaphors, like the irrigation channels that feed and drain a village tank. Valluvar makes a ratio, not an absolute amount, the test of financial health. A narrow inflow (alavu ittidhu, ‘small in measure’) does no harm provided the outflow does not grow broader (agalaak kadai). The verse is often compared to Mr Micawber’s famous rule in Dickens, but it is well over a thousand years older. Within the chapter, it applies ‘knowledge of power’ to the household: one’s economic strength is the relation between inflow and outflow, not the size of either.

tamil:
அளவறிந்து வாழாதான் வாழ்க்கை உளபோல
இல்லாகித் தோன்றாக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Alavarindhu vaazhaadhaan vaazhkkai ulapola
Illaagith thondraak kedum.
current_meaning: The life of one who does not live within the measure of his means will seem to prosper, then vanish without a trace.
elementary_explanation: Someone who spends as if they have more than they do might look rich for a while. But soon it all disappears, as if it had never been there.
university_explanation: The couplet diagnoses an illusion. Ula pola means ‘as if existing’: the spendthrift’s life looks abundant, but it illaagi (becomes nothing) and thondraak kedum (perishes without a trace, not even appearing afterwards). The phrase alavu arindhu vaazhaadhaan ties personal finance back to the chapter’s thesis: living well requires knowledge of one’s measure just as war does. The warning is less about spending itself than about the gap between appearance and substance. Wealth that is not measured is only apparent.

tamil:
உளவரை தூக்காத ஒப்புர வாண்மை
வளவரை வல்லைக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Ulavarai thookkaadha oppuravu aanmai
Valavarai vallaik kedum.
current_meaning: Generosity that does not weigh the limits of one’s own resources will quickly exhaust one’s wealth.
elementary_explanation: Helping others is wonderful, but if you give away more than you actually have, soon you’ll have nothing left, not even enough to keep helping.
university_explanation: Oppuravu is the civic virtue of beneficence to which Valluvar devotes chapter 22 (Oppuravu Arithal), where he says that even ruin incurred through beneficence is worth buying by selling oneself (220). Here he adds the prudential counterweight. Ulavarai thookkaadha describes beneficence that does not weigh (thookku, the same balance-verb as in 471) the extent of what one has, and it rapidly (vallai) destroys the limits of one’s wealth (valavarai). The chapter thus ends where it began, with weighing. Even virtue has to be measured against capacity if it is to last.

tamil:
பகல்வெல்லும் கூகையைக் காக்கை இகல்வெல்லும்
வேந்தர்க்கு வேண்டும் பொழுது.
transliteration:
Pakalvellum Kookaiyaik Kaakkai Ikalvellum
Vendharkku Ventum Pozhudhu.
current_meaning: By day even a crow can beat the stronger owl. A king who means to beat his enemies must likewise wait for the time that favours him.
elementary_explanation: An owl is bigger and fiercer than a crow, but owls can hardly see in bright daylight. So in the daytime a crow can chase an owl away. If you pick the moment when you are at your best and the other side is at its weakest, even a small player can win.
university_explanation: The opening couplet grounds the chapter in natural observation. The kookai (owl) is stronger than the kaakkai (crow), but it is day-blind, so pakal (daytime) reverses their strength. Parimelazhagar draws the lesson for the vendhar (king): an ikal (hostile contest) is won not by strength alone but by the pozhudhu (hour) that suits one’s side. The image has a close Sanskrit parallel in the Panchatantra’s third book, the war of the crows and owls (Kākolūkīya), where the crows burn the owls’ cave by daylight. Both editions consulted (Thirukkural.net and Project Madurai) give the same text, apart from a sandhi spacing in ikalvellum.

tamil:
பருவத்தோடு ஒட்ட ஒழுகல் திருவினைத்
தீராமை ஆர்க்குங் கயிறு.
transliteration:
Paruvaththotu Otta Ozhukal Thiruvinaith
Theeraamai Aarkkung Kayiru.
current_meaning: Acting in step with the season is the rope that ties Fortune down so she cannot slip away.
elementary_explanation: Farmers plant when the rains come, not whenever they like. If you do things at the right time, good luck stays with you as if tied by a rope. If you ignore the time, it wanders off.
university_explanation: Paruvam means season or ripe time, and otta ozhukal means conducting oneself so as to cling to it. The image in the second line is striking: thiru (Fortune, often personified as the goddess Lakshmi or Tirumakal) is fickle by nature, and timely action is the kayiru (rope) that aarkkum (binds) her so that she does not theeraamai, that is, depart. Parimelazhagar glosses paruvam as the time suited to the undertaking. He reads the couplet as a claim that wealth lasts only when action keeps pace with circumstance. Renaissance Europe has a close analogue in Machiavelli’s Fortuna, who favours the man whose conduct matches the times. The Tamil text is identical in both sources consulted.

tamil:
அருவினை யென்ப உளவோ கருவியான்
காலம் அறிந்து செயின்.
transliteration:
Aruvinai Yenpa Ulavo Karuviyaan
Kaalam Arindhu Seyin.
current_meaning: Is there any task that can really be called impossible, if one acts with the proper means and at the proper time?
elementary_explanation: Opening a tight jar is hard with bare hands. With the right tool and a little warm water it is easy. Most ‘impossible’ jobs become possible when you have the right tools and choose the right moment.
university_explanation: The couplet is a rhetorical question: aruvinai enpa ulavo, ‘are there things one could call hard deeds?’ The condition has two parts, karuviyaan (by means of instruments) and kaalam arindhu (knowing the time). Parimelazhagar takes karuvi to mean the resources of the state, such as army and treasury, together with the right methods. Neither timing without means nor means without timing is enough. The printed spelling ‘yenpa’ reflects sandhi with the preceding vowel; the word is enpa.

tamil:
ஞாலம் கருதினுங் கைகூடுங் காலம்
கருதி இடத்தாற் செயின்.
transliteration:
Gnaalam Karudhinung Kaikootung Kaalam
Karudhi Itaththaar Seyin.
current_meaning: Even if you aim at the whole world, it will come within your grasp, provided you choose the right time and act in the right place.
elementary_explanation: A surfer can ride a huge wave, but only by paddling out at the right moment and at the right spot. Pick the right time and place, and even very big goals become reachable.
university_explanation: Gnaalam karudhinum means ‘even if one sets one’s mind on the earth’, that is, universal dominion, and kaikoodum means ‘it will come into one’s hand’. The condition joins kaalam karudhi (considering the time) with idaththaal seyin (acting by means of the place). This anticipates the next chapter, Idanarithal (Knowing the Place, Kurals 491–500). Parimelazhagar explains that idam here means a place of action favourable to oneself and difficult for the enemy. Time and place are treated as the two coordinates of successful action, as in the kāla and deśa of Sanskrit statecraft. Both sources give identical text; ‘karudhinung’ carries the nasal sandhi of karudhinum before k-.

tamil:
காலம் கருதி இருப்பர் கலங்காது
ஞாலம் கருது பவர்.
transliteration:
Kaalam Karudhi Iruppar Kalangaadhu
Gnaalam Karudhu Pavar.
current_meaning: Those who aim at the world wait calmly, unshaken, watching for their time.
elementary_explanation: A cat watching a mouse-hole sits very still and doesn’t get upset or jump too early. People with big goals are like that. They stay calm and wait for their chance.
university_explanation: The couplet picks up gnaalam karudhu (‘aiming at the world’) from the previous kural and shows the inner attitude that goes with it. Such people iruppar, ‘stay’ or ‘sit still’, and do so kalangaadhu, ‘without being agitated’. Parimelazhagar explains that they are not disturbed by the enemy’s present prosperity or by their own present setbacks, because they know that the favourable time will come. The virtue described is patience that is also watchfulness, an active waiting rather than inertia. The printed division ‘karudhu pavar’ is a metrical split of karudhupavar, and the two sources agree.

tamil:
ஊக்க முடையான் ஒடுக்கம் பொருதகர்
தாக்கற்குப் பேருந் தகைத்து.
transliteration:
Ookka Mutaiyaan Otukkam Porudhakar
Thaakkarkup Perun Thakaiththu.
current_meaning: When an energetic man holds back, it is like a fighting ram stepping back so that it can charge harder.
elementary_explanation: When a ram wants to butt, it first walks backward a few steps, then rushes forward with great force. A strong person who waits quietly for a while is not giving up. They are getting ready to charge.
university_explanation: Ookkam means energy or zeal, and otukkam means drawing in, withdrawal or restraint. Porudhakar is a fighting ram (poru, ‘fight’, + thakar, ‘ram’), and thaakkal means butting or striking. Perum thakaiththu means ‘is of the nature of drawing back’, which Parimelazhagar reads as backing up to strike harder. The image reassures anyone who might misread the patient man’s restraint as weakness: his pause is how he gathers force. The same logic appears in the feigned retreats of military history and in Sun Tzu’s ‘coyness of a maiden’ followed by the rush of a hare. The printed ‘perun thakaiththu’ shows the nasal sandhi of perum before th-.

tamil:
பொள்ளென ஆங்கே புறம்வேரார் காலம்பார்த்து
உள்வேர்ப்பர் ஒள்ளி யவர்.
transliteration:
Pollena Aange Puramveraar Kaalampaarththu
Ulverppar Olli Yavar.
current_meaning: The wise do not blaze up in anger on the spot. They keep it inside and wait for the right time.
elementary_explanation: If someone is rude to you and you shout back at once, you may make things worse. A wise person stays calm on the outside, remembers what happened, and deals with it later at a better moment.
university_explanation: Pollena means suddenly or at once, and aange means right there. Puram veraar means ‘they do not sweat or seethe outwardly’, and ul verppar means ‘they seethe within’. Olliyavar are the bright or clear-minded. Parimelazhagar explains that when the wise are provoked by enemies, they do not show anger immediately, because doing so would warn the enemy. They hold it until kaalam paarththu, ‘watching for the time’. The couplet is about strategy, not ethical renunciation of anger: the feeling is kept and redirected, not dissolved. Commentators contrast it with Chapter 31 (Vekulaamai, ‘Not Being Angry’), where anger is to be given up entirely. The two sources agree; ‘olli yavar’ is a metrical split of olliyavar.

tamil:
செறுநரைக் காணின் சுமக்க இறுவரை
காணின் கிழக்காம் தலை.
transliteration:
Serunaraik Kaanin Sumakka Iruvarai
Kaanin Kizhakkaam Thalai.
current_meaning: When you meet your foes, bear with them, even show them deference. When their time of downfall comes, their heads will roll.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes you have to put up with someone difficult who is stronger than you right now. If you stay patient, a time will come when they lose their power. Wait for that time instead of starting a fight you can’t win.
university_explanation: Serunar are enemies, and sumakka means ‘carry’ or ‘bear’. Parimelazhagar understands this as even showing them deference, carrying them ‘on one’s head’ as it were. Iruvarai is the limit or end-time, the point at which the enemy’s fortune has run out. Kizhakkaam thalai, ‘the head will turn downward’, comes from kizh (below). Parimelazhagar reads kizhakku here as keezh, ‘downward’, not the homonym meaning ‘east’. The advice is openly realpolitik: submit outwardly while weak and strike when the enemy’s time has come. It closely echoes Kanika’s counsel to Dhritarashtra in the Mahābhārata to carry the enemy on one’s shoulder and then smash him like a pot on a stone. Both sources give identical text.

tamil:
எய்தற் கரியது இயைந்தக்கால் அந்நிலையே
செய்தற் கரிய செயல்.
transliteration:
Eydhar Kariyadhu Iyaindhakkaal Annilaiye
Seydhar Kariya Seyal.
current_meaning: When a rare opportunity arrives, seize it at once and do the deed that would otherwise be too hard to do.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a gate that opens only for a moment. If you run through right away, you get in. If you wait to think it over, it shuts. When a rare chance comes, use it straight away.
university_explanation: The couplet uses a chiasmus of ‘rare’ things: eydhar kariyadhu (what is hard to obtain, the rare opportunity) and seydhar kariya seyal (deeds hard to do). The link is annilaiye, ‘in that very state, at that very moment’. Iyaindhakkaal means ‘when it has come together’ or ‘when it has fallen into place’. Parimelazhagar stresses immediacy: the opportunity will not return, so the difficult act must be done while it lasts. The previous couplets counselled patience, and this one completes them by insisting that patience ends in decisive action. The Greek figure of Kairos, bald behind so that he cannot be grabbed once he has passed, is the classic Western emblem of the same idea. Text identical in both sources; ‘eydhar kariyadhu’ and ‘seydhar kariya’ are metrical splits of eydharkariyadhu and seydharkariya.

tamil:
கொக்கொக்க கூம்பும் பருவத்து மற்றதன்
குத்தொக்க சீர்த்த இடத்து.
transliteration:
Kokkokka Koompum Paruvaththu Matradhan
Kuththokka Seerththa Itaththu.
current_meaning: While the time is not right, stay still like a heron. When the moment is ripe, strike as fast and as surely as its beak.
elementary_explanation: Have you seen a heron fishing? It stands very still in the water for a long time. When a fish swims close, it stabs down in a flash. Be patient like the heron while you wait, and quick like the heron when your chance comes.
university_explanation: The chapter ends with a double simile built on the kokku (heron or crane). In the season of koompum, ‘folding in’ or ‘drawing oneself together’, one should kokku okka, ‘be like the heron’, standing motionless and seemingly asleep. When the time is seerththa, ‘excellent’ or ‘fitting’, one should be like its kuththu (stab). Parimelazhagar notes the pairing of stillness and sudden strike as the model of a king’s conduct toward enemies. The heron also appears in Manusmṛti 7.106 and in the Chāṇakya Nīti as a model of patient concentration, which suggests a shared South Asian stock image. Some texts, including the musical setting on Thirukkural.net, read ‘seerththa vidaththu’ with a glide consonant. The two editions consulted print ‘seerththa idaththu’.

tamil:
தொடங்கற்க எவ்வினையும் எள்ளற்க முற்றும்
இடங்கண்ட பின்அல் லது.
transliteration:
Thodangarka evvinaiyum ellarka mutrum
Idanganda pinnal lathu.
current_meaning: Begin no action against an enemy, and do not look down on him, until you have found ground from which you can surround and overcome him.
elementary_explanation: Before a game of hide-and-seek, a smart player first looks around for the best hiding spot, and never thinks the seeker is too silly to find them. Valluvar says to do the same with any big task: find the right spot first, and never think the other side is weak.
university_explanation: The chapter opens the third member of the triad that runs through chapters 48 to 50: strength (vali), time (kaalam) and now place (idam). The key word is ‘mutrum idam’, a place from which one can encircle or besiege (mutruthal, to surround, to lay siege); Parimelazhagar and the modern word-glosses (for example thirukkural-thamizh.org) take it as the ground suited for investing the enemy. The two prohibitions are joined: ‘thodangarka’ (do not begin) and ‘ellarka’ (do not despise), so over-confidence and bad positioning are treated as a single error. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah take ‘ellarka’ as ‘do not scorn the enemy’, whereas Kalaignar reads it as ‘do not treat the undertaking itself as trivial’, a minor interpretive variant. Older printed texts give the sandhi form ‘தொடங்கற்க வெவ்வினையு மெள்ளற்க’, which modern editions split as ‘எவ்வினையும் எள்ளற்க’.

tamil:
முரண்சேர்ந்த மொய்ம்பி னவர்க்கும் அரண்சேர்ந்தாம்
ஆக்கம் பலவுந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Muranserntha moimbi navarkkum aransernthaam
Aakkam palavun tharum.
current_meaning: Even for people who are already strong in war, fighting from a secure, fortified position brings many extra advantages.
elementary_explanation: Even the strongest kid in a snowball fight does better behind a snow wall. Being strong is good, but being strong and in a safe spot is much better.
university_explanation: ‘Muran’ means hostility or opposition and ‘moimbu’ means strength, so the first line describes people strong enough to take on an enemy. ‘Aran’ is the fortress, one of the six limbs of the state that later gets its own chapter (74, அரண்), and ‘aakkam’ is gain or prosperity. The ‘-um’ (even) in ‘navarkkum’ is the point: position adds to strength and is no substitute for the lack of it, which is why Parimelazhagar reads the verse as saying that even the mighty gain from a secure base. Modern glosses widen ‘aran’ to any safe place of operation, not only a walled fort (thirukkural-thamizh.org: ‘the place of action is safe’). Older printings show the sandhi ‘மொய்ம்பி னவர்க்கு மரண்சேர்ந்தா மாக்கம்’.

tamil:
ஆற்றாரும் ஆற்றி அடுப இடனறிந்து
போற்றார்கண் போற்றிச் செயின்.
transliteration:
Aatraarum aatri adupa idanarinthu
Potraarkan potrich cheyin.
current_meaning: Even the weak become strong enough to defeat their enemies if they choose the right place and keep themselves protected while acting against the foe.
elementary_explanation: A little cat on a high shelf can bat at a big dog that can’t reach it. The cat isn’t stronger, it just picked the right spot. Valluvar says even weak people can win if they choose their spot well and stay safe.
university_explanation: The verse turns on the wordplay ‘aatraarum aatri’: those who lack power (aatraar) come to have it (aatri) and destroy the enemy (adupa). ‘Potraar’ literally means ‘those who do not honour us’, a standard Kural word for enemies, and the next word ‘potri’ (having guarded, taken care) repeats the sound with the opposite meaning. Parimelazhagar reads ‘potri’ as the actor protecting himself, so the conditions for success are knowing the place and staying self-protected. Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah follow this reading; Kalaignar adds the idea of choosing the right place for the attack. The kural spells out what 492 implied: the right place can make up for missing strength, and not merely add to strength one already has.

tamil:
எண்ணியார் எண்ணம் இழப்பர் இடனறிந்து
துன்னியார் துன்னிச் செயின்.
transliteration:
Enniyaar ennam izhappar idanarinthu
Thunniyaar thunnich cheyin.
current_meaning: If those who have found the right place stay close to it and act from it, enemies who planned to beat them will have to drop their plans.
elementary_explanation: A turtle pulled all the way into its shell makes the curious dog give up and walk away. When you are in the right place and stay there, the other side stops trying.
university_explanation: The verse repeats words in pairs: ‘enniyaar ennam’ (the plan of those who planned) and ‘thunniyaar thunni’ (those who reached the place, keeping close to it). ‘Thunnuthal’ means to approach, cling to or stay close; commentators read the second ‘thunni’ as keeping firmly to the chosen ground instead of drifting away from it. Parimelazhagar takes ‘enniyaar’ as enemies who expected to win, and ‘ennam izhappar’ as more than tactical defeat: they give up the intention itself. Kalaignar has the foe not even daring to think of victory, and Pulavar Kesikan takes ‘thunni’ as pressing the battle closely. Where 493 was about winning, this kural is about deterrence: the right position ends the contest before it begins.

tamil:
நெடும்புனலுள் வெல்லும் முதலை அடும்புனலின்
நீங்கின் அதனைப் பிற.
transliteration:
Nedumpunalul vellum muthalai adumpunalin
Neengin athanaip pira.
current_meaning: In deep water the crocodile overpowers other creatures, but once it leaves the water, those same creatures overpower it.
elementary_explanation: A fish is the best swimmer in the pond, but put it on the grass and it can hardly move. The crocodile is the same: a champion in the river, in trouble on dry land.
university_explanation: This is the chapter’s best-known image. ‘Nedumpunal’ is deep or wide water; ‘adum’ (kills, overcomes) is placed in the middle so that it can be read with either half. Parimelazhagar’s construction is: in deep water the crocodile defeats others; if it leaves the water, others (pira) kill it. The verse leaves out the verb of the second clause and borrows it from ‘adum’, typical Kural compression. The Sanskrit nīti tradition has the same image in a Pañcatantra verse (nakraḥ svasthānam āsādya gajendram api karṣati), where the crocodile in its own place drags even a lordly elephant but out of it is beaten by a dog. That suggests a shared South Asian stock of proverbs rather than direct borrowing.

tamil:
கடலோடா கால்வல் நெடுந்தேர் கடலோடும்
நாவாயும் ஓடா நிலத்து.
transliteration:
Kadalodaa kaalval nedunther kadalodum
Naavaayum odaa nilaththu.
current_meaning: A tall chariot with strong wheels cannot run on the sea, and a ship that sails the sea cannot run on land.
elementary_explanation: A bicycle is great on the road but useless in a swimming pool, and a boat is great in the pool but useless on the road. Every tool, and every person, has a place where it works best.
university_explanation: The kural uses a paired image: ‘kaal val nedunther’, the tall chariot with strong wheels (kaal, literally ‘leg’, here the wheel), and ‘naavaay’, the sea-going ship, a word related to Sanskrit nau and Latin navis, which shows early Tamil familiarity with maritime trade. The repeated verb ‘odaa’ (will not run) connects the two lines. Parimelazhagar reads the verse as an allegory for forces: land armies and naval forces each succeed only in their own element, so a king must match his forces to the terrain. Kalaignar makes it a general lesson that whoever chooses where to act must at least know that a chariot will not cross the sea. The thirukkural-thamizh.org gloss extends it to countries bordered by mountains, forests, sea or desert, each needing its own methods.

tamil:
அஞ்சாமை அல்லால் துணைவேண்டா எஞ்சாமை
எண்ணி இடத்தால் செயின்.
transliteration:
Anjaamai allaal thunaivendaa enjaamai
Enni idaththaal seyin.
current_meaning: If you think everything through without leaving anything out and act from the right place, you need no other ally except fearlessness.
elementary_explanation: If you have practised your speech, checked every page, and are standing in the right spot on stage, the only thing left to bring is courage. This kural says good planning and the right place leave you needing only a brave heart.
university_explanation: ‘Enjaamai enni’ means to think things through without remainder (enjuthal, to be left over), so planning comes first. ‘Idaththaal seyin’ means acting from, or by means of, the right place; the instrumental ‘-aal’ makes place the means of action. ‘Anjaamai allaal thunai vendaa’ says no ally is needed except fearlessness, so courage takes the place of all outside help. Parimelazhagar notes that thorough deliberation and the right ground remove the need for allies (thunai), which were discussed earlier under ‘Valiyarithal’ (ch. 48, thunaivali). Kalaignar’s gloss is about thorough method and leaves out place, a lighter reading than the traditional one.

tamil:
சிறுபடையான் செல்லிடம் சேரின் உறுபடையான்
ஊக்கம் அழிந்து விடும்.
transliteration:
Sirupadaiyaan sellidam serin urupadaiyaan
Ookkam azhinthu vidum.
current_meaning: If a commander with a small army stands on ground where his strength counts, the commander of a large army will lose his drive and his advantage.
elementary_explanation: In a narrow hallway, one kid can block the way even if ten kids are trying to get through, because only one can squeeze in at a time. A small team in the right spot can stop a big team.
university_explanation: ‘Sellidam’ is the key word: ‘the place where one’s power prevails’ (sellu, to be current or valid, as with a coin that ‘passes’). Parimelazhagar reads it as ground favourable to the small army, where it can fight on its own terms. ‘Urupadaiyaan’ is the commander of a large or mighty army, and ‘ookkam’, his drive and self-confidence (the subject of chapter 60), is what gets destroyed. Solomon Pappaiah gives a different reading: when the large army goes after the small one into the place where the small one lies, the large army’s prestige is lost. The sense stays the same, but the grammar of ‘sellidam’ is read in another way.

tamil:
சிறைநலனும் சீரும் இலரெனினும் மாந்தர்
உறைநிலத்தோடு ஒட்டல் அரிது.
transliteration:
Sirainalanum seerum ilareninum maanthar
Urainilaththodu ottal arithu.
current_meaning: Even people who have no strong fort and no special strength are hard to beat when you attack them in the land where they live.
elementary_explanation: Even a small puppy barks bravely and is hard to chase out of its own house, because it knows every corner. People are hardest to beat at home.
university_explanation: ‘Sirai nalan’ is the excellence of an enclosure or defensive barrier (sirai also means a moat or a prison-wall), and ‘seer’ is any other kind of distinction or strength. ‘Urainilam’ is the land where people live, their home ground, and ‘ottal’ is read by Parimelazhagar as going there to engage them. The kural balances 492: there the advantage came from fortification, here it comes from simply being at home, with the home fighter’s knowledge of the land and motivation. The thirukkural-thamizh.org gloss makes the psychology explicit: the knowledge that one is defending one’s own place is itself a source of courage. The verse also works as a warning to the invader, who is always at a disadvantage on foreign ground.

tamil:
காலாழ் களரில் நரியடும் கண்ணஞ்சா
வேலாள் முகத்த களிறு.
transliteration:
Kaalaazh kalaril nariyadum kannanjaa
Velaal mukaththa kaliru.
current_meaning: A fearless war elephant that has impaled spear-carrying soldiers on its tusks can be killed even by jackals once it is stuck in mud where its feet sink.
elementary_explanation: A huge elephant is the strongest animal in the forest, but if it gets stuck in deep mud, even small animals can bother it and it can’t fight back. Being big and strong doesn’t help if you’re stuck in the wrong place.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with its strongest contrast. ‘Kaal aazh kalar’ is mire or saline swamp where legs sink; ‘kann anjaa’ is ‘unflinching of eye’, never afraid; ‘velaal mukaththa kaliru’ is the tusker that carries spear-bearing warriors (velaal) impaled on its tusks (mukam, the front), which Parimelazhagar explains as an elephant that has gored armed soldiers. The ‘nari’ is the jackal, the most contemptible of predators, so the verse sets the mightiest animal against the meanest. The old continuous text (thirukkural-thamizh.org) shows the sandhi ‘காலாழ் களரி னரியடுங் கண்ணஞ்சா வேலாண் முகத்த களிறு’, where ‘வேலாண்’ is ‘வேலாள்’ joined to ‘முகத்த’. The kural returns to 491’s warning: the greatest strength, put on the wrong ground, falls to the weakest enemy.

tamil:
அறம்பொருள் இன்பம் உயிரச்சம் நான்கின்
திறந்தெரிந்து தேறப் படும்.
transliteration:
Aramporul inbam uyirachcham naankin
Thirandherindhu thaerap padum.
current_meaning: A person should be trusted with office only after being examined in four ways: how he behaves when tempted through virtue, through wealth, through pleasure, and through fear for his own life.
elementary_explanation: Before a coach makes someone team captain, she quietly watches: Do they play fair even when cheating would win? Do they share the snacks? Do they get distracted by fun and forget practice? Do they stay brave when things get scary? Only a kid who passes all four gets the armband.
university_explanation: The chapter title pairs தெரிதல் (examining, discerning) with தெளிதல் (arriving at clear confidence), and this opening couplet names the method: testing by the four ‘ways’ (திறம்) of அறம், பொருள், இன்பம் and உயிரச்சம். Parimelazhagar reads these as deliberate trials of the candidate’s mind, a reading made vivid by Solomon Pappaiah, who describes staged provocations on grounds of righteousness, money and a woman’s supposed affection, plus a feigned threat to life. This matches almost point for point Kautilya’s four upadhās (religious, monetary, love and fear allurements) in Arthaśāstra 1.10, and commentators have long noted the correspondence. Kalaignar instead turns the tests into positive qualities (firm in dharma, honest in money, not infatuated by pleasure, unafraid for one’s life). Both web sources give the couplet identically; the final verb தேறப்படும் (‘is to be trusted’) sets the key root தேறு that recurs through the chapter.

tamil:
குடிப்பிறந்து குற்றத்தின் நீங்கி வடுப்பரியும்
நாணுடையான் சுட்டே தெளிவு.
transliteration:
Kudippirandhu kutraththin neengi vaduppariyum
Naanudaiyaan sutte thelivu.
current_meaning: Place your confidence in someone from a good family, who is free of faults and has the sense of shame that dreads any stain on his name.
elementary_explanation: Think about who you would let hold the class pet over the weekend. You would pick the kid from a caring home, who does not break rules, and who would feel really bad if people thought they had been careless. Feeling embarrassed about doing wrong is actually a superpower that keeps people honest.
university_explanation: Three qualifications are stacked: birth in a good lineage (குடிப்பிறப்பு), freedom from faults (குற்றம்), and நாண், the moral shame that fears a வடு, literally a scar, meaning a stain on one’s reputation. சுட்டே தெளிவு means ‘confidence rests on the one so pointed out’. Varadarasan and Pappaiah read குடி as literal family background, while Kalaignar reverses the logic: one who is faultless and ashamed of wrongdoing is thereby shown to be truly ‘high-born’, a reading that plays down birth in favour of conduct. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the first phrase as removing the faults of one’s birth-group. Both sources agree on the text; the idea of நாண் as a guard against wrongdoing returns at length in chapter 102 (நாணுடைமை).

tamil:
அரியகற்று ஆசற்றார் கண்ணும் தெரியுங்கால்
இன்மை அரிதே வெளிறு.
transliteration:
Ariyakatru aasatraar kannum theriyungaal
Inmai aridhe veliru.
current_meaning: Even among people who have studied difficult works and seem free of flaws, close examination will rarely find one without some ignorance.
elementary_explanation: Even the smartest kid in class, the one who knows every dinosaur name, might not know how to tie their shoes. Nobody knows everything. So when you choose someone for a job, check carefully instead of assuming they are perfect.
university_explanation: The couplet tempers the previous two: even the learned (அரிய கற்று) and flawless (ஆசு அற்றார்) will, on examination (தெரியுங்கால்), rarely be found without வெளிறு. வெளிறு literally means ‘whiteness’ and is used of weak, pale timber, and commentators gloss it as அறியாமை (ignorance) or a hidden weak spot. The practical lesson is that selection is not a search for a perfect person but a realistic judgment, which sets up the weighing of strengths and faults in the next couplet (504). Varadarasan and Pappaiah stress that no one is wholly free of ignorance, while Kalaignar aims the point at reputation: even those praised as flawless cannot be assumed so without examination. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
குணம்நாடிக் குற்றமும் நாடி அவற்றுள்
மிகைநாடி மிக்க கொளல்.
transliteration:
Kunamnaadik kutramum naadi avatrul
Migainaadi mikka kolal.
current_meaning: Look into a person’s virtues, then look into his faults, then see which of the two outweighs the other, and judge him by what prevails.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a friend who sometimes forgets your birthday but always shares, always helps, and always tells the truth. If you put the good things on one side of a see-saw and the forgetful thing on the other, the good side sinks way down. That’s how the Kural says to judge people: by which side is heavier.
university_explanation: The verb நாடு (to seek, look into) occurs three times, giving a three-step procedure: examine குணம் (good qualities), then குற்றம் (faults), then மிகை (which is greater), and finally கொளல், ‘take’ the person according to what is மிக்க (predominant). Following 503’s point that no one is flawless, this is a rule of proportion rather than perfection. Pappaiah narrows it to appointment (choose by the excess of virtues), while Kalaignar keeps it general: a clear judgment about someone comes only after this weighing. Some commentators note the ambiguity of மிக்க கொளல்: judge the person by what predominates, or keep the one in whom virtues predominate; either way the method is the same. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
பெருமைக்கும் ஏனைச் சிறுமைக்கும் தத்தம்
கருமமே கட்டளைக் கல்.
transliteration:
Perumaikkum aenaich chirumaikkum thaththam
Karumame kattalaik kal.
current_meaning: For greatness and for its opposite, meanness, each person’s own deeds are the touchstone.
elementary_explanation: A jeweller checks whether a ring is real gold by rubbing it on a special black stone and looking at the streak. You can check whether someone is really kind the same way, by looking at what they actually do, not what they say or what they wear.
university_explanation: கட்டளைக் கல் is the goldsmith’s touchstone (உரைகல்): gold rubbed on it leaves a streak whose colour shows its purity. The couplet says that deeds (கருமம், from Sanskrit karma) are such a stone for both பெருமை (greatness) and சிறுமை (meanness), and the emphatic ஏ in கருமமே excludes other tests such as birth, wealth or eloquence. It completes the lesson of 502: family is a starting presumption, but conduct is the decisive proof. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads கட்டளைக் கல் as an inscribed ‘edict stone’ that guides conduct, but the touchstone reading of Varadarasan, Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Pope (‘touchstone true’) is standard. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
அற்றாரைத் தேறுதல் ஓம்புக மற்றவர்
பற்றிலர் நாணார் பழி.
transliteration:
Atraaraith thaerudhal ombuga matravar
Patrilar naanaar pazhi.
current_meaning: Avoid placing trust in those who have no ties of kin or community, for having no attachments they feel no shame at disgrace.
elementary_explanation: Why do people usually behave well? Partly because they don’t want to let down their family, friends and neighbours. Someone who doesn’t care about anyone might not care if they get in trouble either. So the Kural says: be careful before trusting someone who has no one they care about.
university_explanation: அற்றார் means ‘those who are cut off’; the standard commentary (followed by Varadarasan, Pappaiah and Pope) takes it as those without kin (சுற்றம்), who are therefore பற்றிலர், without attachments, and so நாணார் பழி, unashamed of blame. The reasoning links back to 502: shame works through the people whose opinion one values, so someone with no such bonds has no brake. Kalaignar reads அற்றார் as the unprincipled (நெறியற்றவர்), and Sivayogi Sivakumar reverses the sense, reading it as a call to raise up those who have nothing, a reading at odds with the chapter’s context. ஓம்புக here means ‘guard against, avoid’. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
காதன்மை கந்தா அறிவறியார்த் தேறுதல்
பேதைமை எல்லாந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Kaadhanmai kandhaa arivariyaarth thaerudhal
Paedhaimai ellaan tharum.
current_meaning: To trust people who lack the knowledge they need, merely because you are fond of them, brings every kind of folly.
elementary_explanation: Your best friend is awesome, but if they’ve never baked anything, you wouldn’t make them in charge of the cake for the whole school fair just because you like them. Liking someone is not the same as them being good at the job.
university_explanation: காதன்மை கந்தா means ‘with affection as the post’: கந்து is the post or pillar to which something is tied, so affection becomes the only support of the choice. அறிவு அறியார், ‘those who do not know what should be known’, names the risk, and the result is பேதைமை எல்லாம், every kind of folly. Pappaiah reads it as the folly produced by favouritism in appointments, and Kalaignar adds that such choices bear only useless results. Varadarasan’s printed gloss says the chooser’s ‘ignorance will perish’, which appears to be a typographical slip given his other readings and Pope’s ‘the height of folly’. The text reads எல்லாந் தரும் (sandhi of எல்லாம் + தரும்) in both sources.

tamil:
தேரான் பிறனைத் தெளிந்தான் வழிமுறை
தீரா இடும்பை தரும்.
transliteration:
Thaeraan piranaith thelindhaan vazhimurai
Theeraa idumbai tharum.
current_meaning: Whoever puts confidence in a stranger without examining him brings endless sorrow, even on his descendants.
elementary_explanation: If a stranger at the park says, “Give me your house key and I’ll water your plants,” and you just hand it over, trouble could follow your whole family for a long time. Trust has to be earned before you give it.
university_explanation: தேரான் (‘without examining’) and பிறன் (‘another, an outsider’) define the fault, and தெளிந்தான் (‘he who trusted’) the one who commits it. The key phrase வழிமுறை is read by Varadarasan and Kalaignar as ‘those who come after him’, his descendants, so the harm outlives the one who made the mistake; Pope follows this (‘on all his race’). Pappaiah shifts பிறன் to someone indifferent to the nation’s interests, a modern political reading. The second line தீரா இடும்பை தரும் is repeated word for word in 510, framing the chapter’s last three couplets with the same warning. ytamizh prints the couplet without the final full stop; the words are otherwise identical in both sources.

tamil:
தேறற்க யாரையும் தேராது தேர்ந்தபின்
தேறுக தேறும் பொருள்.
transliteration:
Thaerarka yaaraiyum thaeraadhu thaerndhapin
Thaeruga thaerum porul.
current_meaning: Trust no one without examining him; once you have examined him, trust him in the matters in which he can be trusted.
elementary_explanation: Before you lend your favourite bike, you watch how your cousin treats their own toys. Once you’ve seen they’re careful, you lend it without nagging them every five minutes. Check first, then really trust.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on two nearly identical roots: தேர் (to examine, choose) and தேறு (to trust, be confident). Almost every word is built on them, a characteristic Valluvar wordplay that makes the rule easy to remember: தேறற்க … தேராது (do not trust without examining), தேர்ந்தபின் தேறுக (after examining, trust). The closing phrase தேறும் பொருள் is read in two ways: Varadarasan and Kalaignar take it as trusting in what deserves trust, while the older commentary followed by Pope takes it as entrusting to each person the duties suited to what the test showed. Pappaiah adds the practical corollary that one should not doubt someone after appointing them, which leads into 510. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
தேரான் தெளிவும் தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவும்
தீரா இடும்பை தரும்.
transliteration:
Thaeraan thelivum thelindhaankan aiyuravum
Theeraa idumbai tharum.
current_meaning: Trusting someone you have not examined, and doubting someone you have examined and trusted, both bring endless trouble.
elementary_explanation: There are two ways to mess up with friends. One is trusting someone you just met with a big secret. The other is having a friend who has always been loyal and still checking their bag every day. Both make life miserable. Check carefully once, then trust.
university_explanation: The closing couplet names two opposite errors: தேரான் தெளிவு, confidence without examination (the fault of 508), and தெளிந்தான்கண் ஐயுறவு, suspicion toward someone already tested and trusted. Both produce தீரா இடும்பை, ‘unending affliction’, repeating word for word the second line of 508, so the chapter ends by balancing its warnings: examination is required, but once done it must be honoured. Suspicion of a proven servant damages morale, invites real disloyalty, and wastes the effort of testing, points modern commentators such as Pappaiah and Kalaignar make explicit in the setting of appointments. The next chapter (52, தெரிந்து வினையாடல்) goes on to how the trusted person should be employed. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
நன்மையும் தீமையும் நாடி நலம்புரிந்த
தன்மையான் ஆளப் படும்.
transliteration:
Nanmaiyum theemaiyum naadi nalampurindha
Thanmaiyaan aalap padum.
current_meaning: The person to be employed is the one who, after weighing both the good and the harm in a matter, is by nature drawn to do what is good.
elementary_explanation: Imagine picking a team captain. You don’t pick the kid who just does whatever pops into their head. You pick the one who stops, thinks “what could go right, what could go wrong?”, and then chooses the good way. That’s the kind of person you give a job to.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by naming the first qualification of a worthy agent: not raw talent but a settled disposition (தன்மை) that examines (நாடி) both benefit and harm and then inclines (புரிந்த) toward the good. Varadarasan and Kalaignar read it as a test of the candidate’s character, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as an instruction to the appointee himself — once entrusted with a task, weigh its good and ill and do only what is good. Both readings converge on judgment joined to moral preference: discernment without a love of the good produces a clever but dangerous servant, and good intentions without discernment produce a well-meaning bungler. The pairing anticipates Aristotle’s prohairesis (deliberate choice) and the Upanishadic distinction between the good (śreyas) and the merely pleasant (preyas).

tamil:
வாரி பெருக்கி வளம்படுத்து உற்றவை
ஆராய்வான் செய்க வினை.
transliteration:
Vaari perukki valampaduththu utravai
Aaraaivaan seyga vinai.
current_meaning: Let the work be done by the one who can widen the sources of income, turn them into growing prosperity, and look into and remove the troubles that arise along the way.
elementary_explanation: Think of someone looking after a lemonade stand. A good manager finds more customers, makes the stand earn more, and spots problems early, like running out of cups, and fixes them. That’s the person who should run the stand.
university_explanation: Kural 512 defines administrative competence in three verbs: பெருக்கி (expand the வாரி, the channels of revenue), வளம்படுத்து (turn income into lasting prosperity), and உற்றவை ஆராய் (look into whatever befalls, i.e., foresee and remove obstacles). Parimelazhagar and the modern commentators (Varadarasan, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) all read உற்றவை as the hindrances that threaten wealth, so the ideal agent is productive and protective at once. The couplet is strikingly economic: Valluvar judges the officer by measurable growth, not by birth or favour. Kautilya’s Arthashastra sets out the same standard, promoting superintendents who raise revenue and keeping in permanent service those who increase it loyally.

tamil:
அன்பறிவு தேற்றம் அவாவின்மை இந்நான்கும்
நன்குடையான் கட்டே தெளிவு.
transliteration:
Anbarivu thetram avaavinmai innaankum
Nangudaiyaan katte thelivu.
current_meaning: Trust may safely be placed in the one who fully has these four: loyal love, knowledge, clear and firm judgment, and freedom from greed.
elementary_explanation: If you’re choosing someone to hold the class piggy bank, you want four things: they care about the class, they’re smart, they make clear decisions, and they don’t want the money for themselves. A person with all four is safe to trust.
university_explanation: Kural 513 is a compact job specification: அன்பு (attachment or loyalty to the ruler and the enterprise), அறிவு (knowledge), தேற்றம் (clarity and decisiveness; Varadarasan glosses it as the power to decide without doubt, Kalaignar as capacity to act), and அவாவின்மை (freedom from covetousness). நன்குடையான் stresses that the four must be held fully and steadily, not occasionally. Freedom from greed comes last, as the safeguard that keeps loyalty, knowledge and decisiveness from being turned to private gain. Jethro’s advice to Moses in Exodus 18:21, choosing capable men of truth who hate unjust gain, is an almost exact counterpart.

tamil:
எனைவகையான் தேறியக் கண்ணும் வினைவகையான்
வேறாகும் மாந்தர் பலர்.
transliteration:
Enaivagaiyaan theriyak kannum vinaivagaiyaan
Veraagum maandhar palar.
current_meaning: Even after they have been tested and approved in every possible way, many people turn out differently once they are actually doing the work.
elementary_explanation: Someone can do great in a practice game and then play very differently in the real match. Tests help, but you only really know a person once they’re doing the actual job.
university_explanation: Having spent chapter 51 on testing (தெரிந்து தெளிதல்), Valluvar now admits its limits: however thoroughly a man is examined (எனைவகையான் தேறிய), the nature of the work itself (வினைவகையான்) can change him. Parimelazhagar sees here the corrupting pressure of office, wealth and power, and Pappaiah reads it as simple underperformance against expectations. The practical lesson, developed in Kural 520, is that selection must be followed by continuing supervision. The saying of Bias preserved by Aristotle, “rule will show the man,” states the same insight: power reveals what screening could not.

tamil:
அறிந்தாற்றிச் செய்கிற்பாற்கு அல்லால் வினைதான்
சிறந்தானென்று ஏவற்பாற் றன்று.
transliteration:
Arindhaatrich cheygirpaarku allaal vinaidhaan
Sirandhaanendru evarpaat randru.
current_meaning: A task should be given only to someone who knows how to do it and can push through the difficulties to finish it, never to someone just because he is a favourite or is held in high regard.
elementary_explanation: If the school play needs someone to run the lights, you don’t pick your best friend just because you like them. You pick the kid who knows how the lights work and won’t give up when something goes wrong.
university_explanation: The couplet sets competence against favouritism. Its first line gives the positive standard: அறிந்து (knowing the method), ஆற்றி (enduring obstacles) and செய்கிற்பான் (able to carry the task through). Its second line rules out appointing someone because he is சிறந்தான், someone the ruler holds dear or considers excellent in a general way. Pope’s “specious fav’rite” and Pappaiah’s gloss “thinking him one of our own (party, clan)” bring out the anti-nepotism edge. Plato’s ship of state, where sailors who have never learned navigation clamour to steer, dramatises the same danger.

tamil:
செய்வானை நாடி வினைநாடிக் காலத்தோடு
எய்த உணர்ந்து செயல்.
transliteration:
Seyvaanai naadi vinainaadik kaalaththodu
Eydha unarndhu seyal.
current_meaning: First size up the person who will do the work, then size up the work itself, and then act once you are sure both fit the right time.
elementary_explanation: To bake a cake you need the right baker, the right recipe, and the right moment, so it’s ready when the party starts. Get all three right and it works.
university_explanation: Kural 516 sets out a three-part planning method: examine the doer (செய்வானை நாடி), examine the deed (வினைநாடி), and fit both to the proper time (காலத்தோடு எய்த உணர்ந்து). Pappaiah reads it as bringing agent and task together and then matching the pair to the moment. The couplet also draws on the earlier chapters on strength (48), time (49) and place (50). Plato’s specialisation principle, that things go best when each person does the one thing natural to him and does it at the right time, runs remarkably parallel.

tamil:
இதனை இதனால் இவன்முடிக்கும் என்றாய்ந்து
அதனை அவன்கண் விடல்.
transliteration:
Idhanai idhanaal ivanmudikkum endraaindhu
Adhanai avankan vidal.
current_meaning: Once you have worked out that “this person will get this job done by these means,” hand the job over to him and leave it with him.
elementary_explanation: When your teacher knows you’re good at drawing and have the markers you need, she gives you the class poster to make and then lets you do it, without hovering over every line.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on demonstratives: இதனை (this task), இதனால் (by these means), இவன் (this man), and then அதனை அவன்கண் விடல் (leave that with him). Delegation follows a specific three-way match of task, resources and person; Varadarasan glosses இதனால் as “by this instrument” and Pappaiah as the manpower and money available. விடல் (to release) implies real handing over, not a nominal assignment followed by micromanagement. Jethro’s advice in Exodus 18, and the master in the parable of the talents who gives each servant a share “according to his several ability” and then departs, express the same trust.

tamil:
வினைக்குரிமை நாடிய பின்றை அவனை
அதற்குரிய னாகச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Vinaikkurimai naadiya pindrai avanai
Adharkuriya naagach cheyal.
current_meaning: After you have found out which work a person is suited to, make him fully responsible for that work, with the authority that goes with it.
elementary_explanation: If you find out your friend is the best goalkeeper, you don’t just let them try out. You make them the goalkeeper for real, with the gloves and everything.
university_explanation: The key word is உரிமை, suitability and also rightful ownership. Once fitness for a task (வினைக்குரிமை) has been established, the ruler must make the person its rightful holder (அதற்குரியனாக).
