Pappaiah stresses the second half: having appointed a man, let him exercise the powers of the post himself. The couplet thus balances Kural 517: 517 is about handing over, 518 about conferring the standing and authority that make the handover real. It is Valluvar’s closest statement of the specialisation principle, which Plato made the definition of justice and the Gita discussed in terms of svadharma.

tamil:
வினைக்கண் வினையுடையான் கேண்மைவே றாக
நினைப்பானை நீங்கும் திரு.
transliteration:
Vinaikkan vinaiyudaiyaan kenmaive raaga
Ninaippaanai neengum thiru.
current_meaning: Fortune abandons the ruler who misreads, and grows suspicious of, the closeness of a man who is devoted to the work entrusted to him.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a kid who works really hard on a group project and is friendly with the teacher, and the teacher starts thinking “he must be up to something.” If you treat your best helpers that way, you lose them, and everything goes wrong.
university_explanation: The couplet warns against a failure of trust after appointment. வினைக்கண் வினையுடையான் is the man wholly absorbed in his assigned work; கேண்மை வேறாக நினைத்தல் is to read his familiarity or friendship with the ruler as something else, such as presumption or disloyalty. Pope renders it as failing to bear the informal friendly ways of such servants, and Pappaiah adds the courtly setting of slanderers who poison the ruler’s mind against capable officers. The penalty is that திரு (prosperity, the goddess of fortune) departs, because a ruler who drives away his best workers destroys his own wealth. Saul’s jealousy of David is the classic Hebrew example.

tamil:
நாடோறும் நாடுக மன்னன் வினைசெய்வான்
கோடாமை கோடா துலகு.
transliteration:
Naadorum naaduga mannan vinaiseyvaan
Kodaamai kodaa thulagu.
current_meaning: A king should look into the conduct of those doing his work every day, because as long as they do not go crooked, the world does not go crooked either.
elementary_explanation: A good coach checks on the team at every practice, not just once at the start of the season. If the players stay on track, the whole team does well.
university_explanation: The chapter closes by joining selection to supervision: நாடோறும் நாடுக, examine every day. The logic is causal: if the worker does not swerve (கோடாமை), the world, meaning the realm and its people, will not swerve (கோடாது). Most commentators read it as vigilance over officials, but Kalaignar reads கோடாமை as the worker’s heart not withering, so the king’s daily attention becomes care for the welfare of labour. Kautilya prescribes almost the same thing, that superintendents be examined daily because men are changeable, which gives the Kural a precise parallel in Indian statecraft.

tamil:
பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் பழைமைபா ராட்டுதல்
சுற்றத்தார் கண்ணே உள.
transliteration:
Patratra kannum pazhaimaipaa raattudhal
Sutraththaar kanne ula.
current_meaning: Even when a man has lost everything he owned, only his kin still honour the old bond they shared with him.
elementary_explanation: When someone’s pockets are full, lots of people want to sit next to them at lunch. But if they lose everything, most of those people drift away. Your family is different: they still remember the good times and stay by your side. That is what makes family special.
university_explanation: The chapter title சுற்றம் தழால் means ‘embracing the circle of kin’; Parimelazhagar glosses it as the king holding his kinsmen close so that they never leave him, and he explains that it follows ‘Selection and Employment’ (Ch. 52) because, having spoken of those who do the king’s work, Valluvar now turns to the rest of his ‘surround’. In this opening couplet பற்று means wealth or support, so பற்றற்ற கண்ணும் is ‘even when all holdings are gone’; the concessive உம் implies that such a man is normally no longer honoured by anyone. Parimelazhagar reads பழைமை as the kindnesses the man once did for them in his days of plenty, and the emphatic ஏ in கண்ணே stresses that kin alone keep faith, since others cut ties the moment the wealth is gone. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah and Karunanidhi all agree on the sense, and Karunanidhi turns it into a definition: those who show this loyalty are the true kin. Editions differ only in sandhi (உள / யுள) at the end of the second line.

tamil:
விருப்பறாச் சுற்றம் இயையின் அருப்பறா
ஆக்கம் பலவும் தரும்.
transliteration:
ViruppaRaach chutram iyaiyin aruppaRaa
Aakkam palavum tharum.
current_meaning: If a man is blessed with kin whose love never fails, they will bring him many kinds of prosperity that keep on growing.
elementary_explanation: Think of a garden where lots of people help water the plants. The plants keep growing new branches and flowers. A family that loves you all the time works like those helpers: with them around, good things keep sprouting in your life.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar notes that விருப்பறா (‘whose affection never ceases’) is there to exclude kin who are secret enemies (உட்பகை), and that அருப்பறா qualifies ஆக்கம் to mean wealth that never stops putting out new shoots (அருப்பு, ‘sprouting’, which he glosses as கிளைத்தல், ‘branching’). This separates it from wealth that grows only by its owner’s own effort. He explains the conditional இயையின் (‘if one should obtain’) as a sign of how rare such kin are, and reads பலவும் (‘all the many’) as pointing to the six limbs of the state (army, subjects, treasury, ministers, allies and fortress), which keep growing because many hands tend them together. The couplet sets out the economic logic of the chapter: kin are the root of expanding prosperity. The text is stable, and the Tamil commentators agree on the meaning.

tamil:
அளவளா வில்லாதான் வாழ்க்கை குளவளாக்
கோடின்றி நீர்நிறைந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Alavalaa villaadhaan vaazhkkai kulavalaak
Kotindri neernirain thatru.
current_meaning: The life of a man who does not mix heart to heart with his kin is like a wide tank that fills with water but has no banks: whatever comes in simply runs away.
elementary_explanation: Imagine pouring water into a pond with no edges. The water spreads out and disappears, and the pond never stays full. A person who keeps away from family is like that pond: good things come, but with no one around to help hold on to them, they slip away.
university_explanation: The key word அளவளாவு means intimate mingling, literally ‘measuring together’. Parimelazhagar explains that heart-union grows out of exchanging one’s own measure with another’s, so the word stands by metonymy for close intimacy with kin, and ‘with kin’ is supplied from the chapter heading. குளவளா is the broad expanse of a tank and கோடு is its bank. For Parimelazhagar வாழ்க்கை here stands for the wealth that sustains life, and his point is that without kin to ‘hold’ it, a man’s wealth drains outward just as water spills from a tank that has no banks. He groups kurals 522-524 as showing kin to be the cause (ஏது), the fortress (அரண்) and the fruit (பயன்) of wealth, and this couplet shows kin as the fortress. Some printed texts divide the first word as அளவளாவு இல்லாதான், and thirukkural.net prints it with a space as அளவளா வில்லாதான்.

tamil:
சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப் படஒழுகல் செல்வந்தான்
பெற்றத்தால் பெற்ற பயன்.
transliteration:
Sutraththaal sutrap pataozhukal selvandhaan
Petraththaal petra payan.
current_meaning: The real reward of gaining wealth is to live in such a way that one’s kin gather round one.
elementary_explanation: Suppose you have a big box of snacks. If you eat them alone, it’s just snacks. If you share them, your cousins come and sit around you, laughing and talking. That circle of family is the real prize, not the snacks.
university_explanation: The couplet repeats sounds on purpose (சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப்பட, பெற்றத்தால் பெற்ற) so that the verse itself seems to ‘surround’ its subject. Parimelazhagar glosses it as: the fruit a man gains from having gained wealth is to conduct himself, embracing his kin, so that he is encircled by them. He notes that in பெற்ற the final அ, and in அதனால் the particle அன், have dropped out for the sake of the rhyme. He explains that such conduct counts as the ‘fruit’ of wealth because it lets a king rule without enemies, and he treats it as the third term of the sequence cause–fortress–fruit (kurals 522-524). Pappaiah and Karunanidhi read it the same way. The gloss attributed to Mu. Varadarasan for this kural on thirukkural.net actually belongs to kural 468 and is evidently misplaced there.

tamil:
கொடுத்தலும் இன்சொலும் ஆற்றின் அடுக்கிய
சுற்றத்தால் சுற்றப் படும்.
transliteration:
Kotuththalum insolum aatrin atukkiya
Sutraththaal sutrap patum.
current_meaning: A man who can both give generously and speak kindly will be surrounded by kin, circle after circle of them.
elementary_explanation: If you share your crayons and also say nice things to people, everyone wants to be near you. Then their brothers and sisters come too, and soon there’s a big happy circle around you. Sharing plus kind words is like a magnet for family.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar notes that the verb ஆற்றின் (‘if one is able to accomplish’) stresses how hard it is to practise both virtues in due measure. He explains அடுக்கிய சுற்றம் as kin ‘stacked’ in succession: the kin of one’s kin, and then their kin, bound in a widening chain. He explicitly identifies the two means with the Sanskrit statecraft terms dāna (gift) and sāma (conciliation), the first two of the four upāyas, so this kural brings the Arthaśāstra toolkit into the domestic setting of kinship. Kurals 525-528, he says, set out the ‘means of embracing kin’. இன்சொல் (‘sweet speech’) links back to Chapter 10, இனியவை கூறல், and it anticipates the Buddhist saṅgahavatthu of giving and kind speech.

tamil:
பெருங்கொடையான் பேணான் வெகுளி அவனின்
மருங்குடையார் மாநிலத்து இல்.
transliteration:
Perungotaiyaan penaan vekuli avanin
Marungutaiyaar maanilaththu il.
current_meaning: No one on this great earth has more kin around him than a man who gives freely and does not nurse anger.
elementary_explanation: Picture two kids. One shares a lot but gets angry and shouts all the time. The other shares and stays calm and kind. Everyone flocks to the second kid. Giving plus a calm heart brings the biggest family circle.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar glosses பெருங்கொடை as ‘great liberality’ of a kind that never itself leads to want. He takes பேணான் வெகுளி (‘does not cherish anger’) to mean that the king does not indulge anger beyond measure, since he grants that a ruler may sometimes need to show it. மருங்கு (‘side’) here means kin (கிளை), so மருங்குடையார் are ‘those who have people at their side’. This kural adds a negative condition to the positive means of 525: generosity will not keep kin if it comes with an unpredictable temper, a point that looks ahead to Chapter 31 (வெகுளாமை) and to 306, where anger is said to burn the raft of one’s own people (இனம்). The text is stable, and all the main commentators agree.

tamil:
காக்கை கரவா கரைந்துண்ணும் ஆக்கமும்
அன்னநீ ரார்க்கே உள.
transliteration:
Kaakkai karavaa karaindhunnum aakkamum
Annanee raarkke ula.
current_meaning: A crow does not hide its food; it caws to call its kin and eats with them. Prosperity comes only to people of that same nature.
elementary_explanation: When a crow finds food, it doesn’t sneak off with it. It says ‘Caw! Caw!’ so its whole family comes to share. People who share like the crow end up with the most good things in life, because everyone sticks with them.
university_explanation: This is the best-known couplet of the chapter. Parimelazhagar explains that when crows find food they do not hide it (கரவா) but caw (கரைந்து) to summon their flock and eat together, and that the ‘prosperities’ (ஆக்கமும்) that come through kin belong only to those who have such a nature (அன்ன நீரார்). He lists those prosperities as freedom from enemies and great wealth. He reads the உம் in ஆக்கமும் as an ‘inclusive’ particle: such people gain not only virtue (அறம்) and pleasure (இன்பம்) but material wealth (பொருள்) as well. He defines the crow-like nature as arranging things so that kin enjoy everything one enjoys oneself. Some modern readers (e.g. Karunanidhi) take ஆக்கம் more broadly as ‘elevation’. The crow’s calling of its kin is proverbial in Tamil culture and is echoed in later didactic literature.

tamil:
பொதுநோக்கான் வேந்தன் வரிசையா நோக்கின்
அதுநோக்கி வாழ்வார் பலர்.
transliteration:
Podhunokkaan vendhan varisaiyaa nokkin
Adhunokki vaazhvaar palar.
current_meaning: If a king does not treat everyone the same but gives each person the regard their merit deserves, many will stay by him because they value that recognition.
elementary_explanation: A good coach doesn’t give every player the same job. The fastest runner plays forward, and the one with the best hands becomes goalkeeper. When each person feels truly seen for what they’re good at, they all want to stay on the team.
university_explanation: The couplet contrasts பொது நோக்கு (‘common or uniform regard’) with வரிசை நோக்கு (‘regard according to rank or order’). Parimelazhagar reads வரிசை as each person’s own worth (தத்தம் தகுதி). He explains that uniform treatment is rejected because it drives away the superior, who feel slighted, while graded regard is prescribed because it keeps everyone loyal. This makes it a principle of proportional, not arithmetic, equality, very like Aristotle’s distributive justice. With this kural Parimelazhagar closes the four-verse unit (525-528) on the ‘means of embracing kin’. Karunanidhi’s modern gloss softens the hierarchy (‘all people are equal, but use each according to ability’), and Pappaiah places the kural explicitly within the ruler’s treatment of his kin.

tamil:
தமராகித் தற்றுறந்தார் சுற்றம் அமராமைக்
காரணம் இன்றி வரும்.
transliteration:
Thamaraakith thatrurandhaar sutram amaraamaik
Kaaranam indri varum.
current_meaning: Kin who were once close but left because of some grievance will come back of their own accord once the cause of the rift is gone.
elementary_explanation: Suppose your cousin stopped coming over because you kept teasing him. If you stop teasing, he’ll start coming back all by himself. When you fix the reason someone left, the friendship often heals itself.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar construes the couplet as: when those who were once one’s own (தமர்) have left because of some cause, their becoming kin again ‘comes’ (வரும்) of itself once that cause of discord (அமராமைக் காரணம்) no longer exists in oneself. He infers from the phrase that the cause really did exist before, and names it as the king’s own conduct, such as straying from the right path or doing things that displease. Because the kin were naturally affectionate and the estrangement was artificial, it ends when its cause ends; the ruler need not court them again, since they ‘return’ to their old nature. Pappaiah reads the kural in modern political terms, as members returning to a movement once the leader’s fault is gone. Karunanidhi reads it differently: those who left on some pretext come back once they see the pretext does not hold. Thirukkural.net prints தமராகிக் in the first word, but Parimelazhagar’s text on Wikisource and the standard editions read தமராகித், which is the reading adopted here.

tamil:
உழைப்பிரிந்து காரணத்தின் வந்தானை வேந்தன்
இழைத்திருந்து எண்ணிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Uzhaippirindhu kaaranaththin vandhaanai vendhan
Izhaiththirundhu ennik kolal.
current_meaning: When a kinsman who left the king without cause comes back for some purpose of his own, the king should meet that need, wait, and weigh him carefully before taking him back.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a teammate who quit for no reason and now wants to rejoin because he needs something. The captain can help him, but should watch how he behaves for a while before trusting him fully again. Welcome back, but with open eyes.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar takes the bare உழைப் பிரிந்து (‘having left one’s side’) to imply that there was no reason for leaving, and காரணத்தின் வந்தானை as ‘one who came back because of some purpose’. He explains இழைத்திருந்து as ‘having done or supplied that purpose’: if the king does not meet the motive that brought the man back, he may leave again and join the enemy. He explains எண்ணிக் கொளல் as ‘accept him after examination’, because the man left without love and came back out of interest. Taken together with 529, Parimelazhagar sees two cases: the kinsman whom the king’s own fault drove away should be allowed to return freely, while the one who left without cause should be taken back only after scrutiny. Varadarasan similarly says the king should grant the help sought and then examine before re-admitting him, while Pappaiah reads இழைத்திருந்து as ‘waiting patiently’. Karunanidhi instead describes the man as one who left on a pretext and returned for a genuine reason.

tamil:
இறந்த வெகுளியின் தீதே சிறந்த
உவகை மகிழ்ச்சியிற் சோர்வு.
transliteration:
Irandha vekuliyin theedhe sirandha
Uvakai makizhchchiyir sorvu.
current_meaning: Getting careless because you are carried away by great joy does more harm than even anger that has gone past all limits.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a team that is winning a game by a lot. The players start celebrating early, stop paying attention, and the other team sneaks back and wins. Getting too excited and careless can hurt you even more than losing your temper, because you don't even notice the danger coming.
university_explanation: The chapter title பொச்சாவாமை is the negative verbal noun of பொச்சா- (‘to forget, to be negligent’; compare பொச்சாப்பு, ‘forgetfulness, heedlessness’). So it names a positive discipline of not forgetting, and because it sits in the Arasiyal (royal conduct) section, Parimelazhagar reads the whole chapter as advice to a king. In this couplet சோர்வு is the lapse or slackening born of சிறந்த உவகை மகிழ்ச்சி, ‘the delight of surpassing joy’, and இறந்த வெகுளி is anger that has gone past all bounds. Parimelazhagar says that such joy comes from great wealth, great pleasure and great pride. He explains the comparison this way: measured anger is needed to crush enemies and punish the wicked, and even excessive anger may sometimes kill a foe, but forgetfulness born of joy kills only the person who has it, so it is the worse evil. Manakkudavar agrees on the sense but records another way to read the phrase, as the joy one directs towards those one must favour. Pavanar follows Parimelazhagar. The emphatic ஏ in தீதே underlines the surprising verdict that the pleasant fault is worse than the violent one.

tamil:
பொச்சாப்புக் கொல்லும் புகழை அறிவினை
நிச்ச நிரப்புக்கொன் றாங்கு.
transliteration:
Pochchaappuk kollum pukazhai arivinai
Nichcha nirappuk kon raangu.
current_meaning: Just as grinding, day-after-day poverty kills a person's intelligence, forgetfulness kills a person's good name.
elementary_explanation: If a child is hungry every single day, it is very hard for them to think clearly at school. In the same way, if someone keeps forgetting their promises and jobs, people slowly stop trusting and admiring them, until their good name is gone.
university_explanation: The verb கொல்லும் (‘kills’) does strong work in both halves: பொச்சாப்பு kills புகழ் (fame) just as நிச்ச நிரப்பு kills அறிவு (understanding). Parimelazhagar glosses நிச்ச நிரப்பு as filling one's belly every day by begging. When this happens to a learned man, the humiliation and sin involved bring contempt on him and destroy the regard he enjoyed. In the same way, forgetfulness in a man of fame brings contempt, because he fails to guard himself and his affairs fall apart, and so it destroys his standing. Pavanar notes that நிரப்பு (literally ‘fullness’) is an auspicious euphemism for poverty, and he cross-refers to Kural 1046, where even the sound words of the poor go unheeded. Manakkudavar reads this couplet as part of a set on holding firm in worldly affairs. Parimelazhagar groups 531-532 as the couplets that state the fault of heedlessness. Editions split the final words either as நிரப்புக்கொன் றாங்கு or as நிரப்புக் கொன்றாங்கு; the sense is the same.

tamil:
பொச்சாப்பார்க் கில்லை புகழ்மை அதுஉலகத்து
எப்பால்நூ லோர்க்கும் துணிவு.
transliteration:
Pochchaappaark killai pukazhmai adhuulakaththu
Eppaalnoo lorkkum thunivu.
current_meaning: The forgetful never win lasting fame. On this point, the authors of every kind of treatise in the world agree.
elementary_explanation: Ask a coach, a music teacher, a doctor, or a chef, and they will all tell you the same thing: people who keep forgetting and not paying attention never become great at anything. When everyone agrees on something, it's worth listening!
university_explanation: புகழ்மை means ‘the state of having fame’, and துணிவு here means a settled conclusion, not courage. Parimelazhagar takes எப்பால் நூலோர் to mean the authors of treatises of every kind, not only of polity (நீதி நூல்). He explains that the rule holds for everyone, not only kings: anyone pursuing any of the four aims of life (aṟam, poruḷ, iṉpam, vīṭu) will fail if heedless, and so will have no fame. Pavanar agrees that the rule is universal but argues that உலகம் here means the Tamil world and that எப்பால் நூல் refers to the branches of Tamil learning, much of which has since been lost; he points out that Valluvar does not say the northern (Sanskrit) texts agree. Manakkudavar reads the couplet simply as saying that heedlessness brings no fame. Parimelazhagar groups 533-535 as describing the harm (ஏதம்) that comes to the heedless.

tamil:
அச்ச முடையார்க்கு அரணில்லை ஆங்கில்லை
பொச்சாப் புடையார்க்கு நன்கு.
transliteration:
Achcha mutaiyaarkku aranillai aangillai
Pochchaap putaiyaarkku nanku.
current_meaning: No fortress helps someone who is afraid at heart, and in the same way no advantage helps someone who is heedless.
elementary_explanation: A castle with tall walls won't help a guard who is too scared to stand at his post. And a house full of good locks won't help if you forget to lock the door. What really protects you is what's going on inside your own head.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a simile (உவமை) marked by ஆங்கு (‘in the same way’). Fear inside makes outer defences (அரண்) useless, and forgetfulness inside makes outer goods (நன்கு) useless. Parimelazhagar spells out the அரண் as forest, mountain and similar strongholds, and glosses நன்கு as wealth of every kind, called ‘the good’ because it is a means to good. His conclusion is that just as the stronghold of the fearful falls, the riches of the heedless perish. Pavanar adds armies to the list of advantages and derives நன்கு from நல் > நன். Manakkudavar sums the couplet up as saying that the heedless have no protection. By pairing அச்சம் (fear) with பொச்சாப்பு (heedlessness), Valluvar treats both as inner failures of a ruler's mind that no outward resource can make up for.

tamil:
முன்னுறக் காவாது இழுக்கியான் தன்பிழை
பின்னூறு இரங்கி விடும்.
transliteration:
Munnurak kaavaadhu izhukkiyaan thanpizhai
Pinnooru irangi vitum.
current_meaning: Someone who carelessly fails to guard against trouble before it comes will be left grieving over his own mistake once it strikes.
elementary_explanation: If you know a test is coming and you don't study, you'll feel terrible when you see questions you can't answer. Getting ready before trouble comes is much better than feeling sorry afterwards.
university_explanation: முன் உற (‘before it arrives’) and பின் ஊறு (‘when the blow has fallen’) frame the couplet in time, and இழுக்கியான் (‘one who slipped, was negligent’) is described by காவாது (‘without guarding’). Parimelazhagar says the troubles in view are those that can be guarded against, namely what enemies do when they spot a lapse. He treats ஊறு as standing for ஊற்றின்கண், with both the case-ending and the linking syllable dropped, and explains இரங்கிவிடும் as ‘will be left to grieve’, because once the trouble has come it can no longer be warded off. Pavanar widens the preventable troubles to include famine and flood, and takes விடும் in the sense of ‘perishing’. Manakkudavar's gloss is almost word for word the same as Parimelazhagar's. This couplet closes Parimelazhagar's group of three (533-535) on the harm that comes to the heedless.

tamil:
இழுக்காமை யார்மாட்டும் என்றும் வழுக்காமை
வாயின் அதுவொப்பது இல்.
transliteration:
Izhukkaamai yaarmaattum endrum vazhukkaamai
Vaayin adhuvoppadhu il.
current_meaning: If a person can keep up unfailing watchfulness towards everyone and at all times, no other good can equal it.
elementary_explanation: Being careful once is easy. Being careful with everyone, every day, even when things are going great, is the real superpower. If you can do that, it's better than almost any other gift you could have.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on two near-synonyms: இழுக்காமை (‘not slipping’, that is, unforgetfulness) must be present வழுக்காமை (‘without a lapse’). Parimelazhagar explains யார்மாட்டும் as reaching even the king's own people, the servants who do his work and his kin, and என்றும் as meaning ‘in days of growth and of decline alike’. He parses வாயின் as a conditional form built on the verbal-noun stem வாய் (‘to come right, to fall into place’). Pavanar adds that வழுக்காமை means applying this without fail in every task, and he explicitly rejects Parimelazhagar's analysis of வாயின், citing Tolkāppiyam and Kural 737 to argue that வாய் is an intransitive verb. Manakkudavar reads the couplet as a rule for the careful administration of justice. Together with 537, this couplet forms Parimelazhagar's pair on the excellence of unforgetfulness.

tamil:
அரியஎன்று ஆகாத இல்லைபொச் சாவாக்
கருவியால் போற்றிச் செயின்.
transliteration:
Ariyaendru aakaadha illaipoch chaavaak
Karuviyaal potrich cheyin.
current_meaning: No task is too hard to accomplish, however difficult it is said to be, if a person does it carefully, using an unforgetting mind as the tool.
elementary_explanation: Building a huge Lego castle sounds impossible. But if you keep the picture in your head, follow each step carefully, and don't lose track, you can finish it. A mind that doesn't forget is like a super-tool that makes hard jobs possible.
university_explanation: அரிய என்று ஆகாத இல்லை is a double negative: ‘there is nothing that, being called difficult, cannot be done’. Parimelazhagar takes பொச்சாவாக் கருவி to mean ‘the unforgetting mind’. On his reading, பொச்சாவாத has lost its final syllable by poetic licence, and the mind is called கருவி (‘instrument’) because it is the inner instrument (அந்தக்கரணம்); போற்றிச் செயின் means ‘if one does it with careful thought’. His summary is that people with unbroken attention and sound planning accomplish everything easily. Pavanar calls this gloss over-learned and prefers to read பொச்சாவாக் கருவி as an appositional compound, ‘the instrument that is unforgetfulness’. Manakkudavar likewise glosses it as மறவாமையாகிய கருவி. Modern commentators such as Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah reflect both readings.

tamil:
புகழ்ந்தவை போற்றிச் செயல்வேண்டும் செய்யாது
இகழ்ந்தார்க்கு எழுமையும் இல்.
transliteration:
Pukazhndhavai potrich cheyalventum seyyaadhu
Ikazhndhaarkku ezhumaiyum il.
current_meaning: One must carefully do the things the wise have praised. For those who neglect them and leave them undone, there is no good in any of their seven births.
elementary_explanation: Your teachers and parents tell you some things are really worth doing, like being kind, doing homework, and telling the truth. Knowing that isn't enough; you have to actually do them. People who shrug those things off miss out on good things again and again.
university_explanation: புகழ்ந்தவை means ‘the things praised’. Parimelazhagar identifies them as the duties that works on polity single out as proper to kings: the three powers, the four expedients (upāya), the five kinds of action, the six policies, and so on. இகழ்ந்தார் here does not mean ‘those who scorned’; all the commentators take it as ‘those who neglected or forgot’, and Parimelazhagar glosses it as மறந்தவர். He reads எழுமையும் இல் as ‘no good in all seven births’, on the ground that those who fall away from their proper duty reap only suffering in hell, and he treats எழுமை (‘sevenfoldness’) as a metonymy. Pavanar rejects Parimelazhagar's appeal to caste duty (சாதி தருமம்) as foreign to the text, lists instead celebrated deeds of the ancient Tamil kings as examples of ‘praised acts’, and reads எழுமை as a conventional number. Parimelazhagar says this couplet sets out what must be done without forgetting.

tamil:
இகழ்ச்சியின் கெட்டாரை உள்ளுக தாந்தம்
மகிழ்ச்சியின் மைந்துறும் போழ்து.
transliteration:
Ikazhchchiyin kettaarai ulluka thaandham
Makizhchchiyin maindhurum pozhdhu.
current_meaning: Whenever you feel strong and swollen with your own delight, remember those who were ruined through heedlessness.
elementary_explanation: When you win a prize and feel like the best in the world, it's a good moment to remember the story of the hare who was so sure of winning that he took a nap and lost to the tortoise. Remembering other people's mistakes keeps you careful.
university_explanation: இகழ்ச்சி here means heedless disregard (it shares a root with இகழ்ந்தார் in 538), and மைந்துறும் போழ்து means ‘the moment one grows strong or elated’. Parimelazhagar makes kings the subject: when they grow confident in their own pleasures, they should remember those of old who perished through the lapse such pleasure breeds. He explains that the text says ‘their own delight’ because the king owns the means of pleasure, and that it ties elation to ruin because neglect and downfall arise together. The point, he says, is that one who recalls the ruined will think ‘I too shall perish that way’ and will not grow elated. He also records a variant reading, எண்ணுக for உள்ளுக, which Pavanar attributes to Manakkudavar. Manakkudavar gives the couplet a concrete application: kings should have their food, clothing and unguents examined, that is, guard against poisoning.

tamil:
உள்ளியது எய்தல் எளிதுமன் மற்றுந்தான்
உள்ளியது உள்ளப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Ulliyadhu eydhal elidhuman matrundhaan
Ulliyadhu ullap perin.
current_meaning: Reaching what you have set your mind on is easy, as long as you can keep thinking of it steadily from then on.
elementary_explanation: If you want to learn to ride a bike, you have to keep that goal in your mind every day, even after you fall. Kids who keep thinking about their goal and don't let it slip away usually get there.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on repeating உள்ளியது (‘what was thought of’) together with the verb உள்ளு (‘to think of, keep in mind’): attaining your aim is easy if you can ‘think again what you thought’. Parimelazhagar reads it as advice to a king: he will easily obtain what he intended, exactly as he intended it, if he can keep thinking of that same thing, which he explains as striving towards it without forgetting. He takes மன் as an ஒழியிசை particle, one that implies an unspoken ‘but that is hard to manage’, so the couplet quietly admits that sustained attention is the difficult part. Pavanar rejects this analysis of மன் as unsuitable here and takes மற்று to mean ‘afterwards, further’. Manakkudavar reads the couplet as the requirement to remember, above all, what one first resolved. Parimelazhagar groups 539-540 as the means (உபாயம்) for achieving unforgetfulness.

tamil:
ஓர்ந்துகண் ணோடாது இறைபுரிந்து யார்மாட்டும்
தேர்ந்துசெய் வஃதே முறை.
transliteration:
Orndhukan Notaadhu Iraipurindhu Yaarmaattum
Therndhusey Vaqdhe Murai.
current_meaning: Justice means looking into every case with care, showing no favour to anyone, holding to fairness, and acting only after the matter has been weighed with people who know the law.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a teacher who finds two kids fighting over a broken toy. A fair teacher doesn’t just blame the kid she likes less. She asks questions, listens to both, thinks it over, and then decides. Even if the one who broke it is her favourite helper, the rule is the same for him. That is what “doing it the right way” means.
university_explanation: This opening couplet works as a definition: முறை (justice, right order) is a four-step procedure. ஓர்ந்து means investigating what offence was committed; கண்ணோடாது means without கண்ணோட்டம், the soft favour that comes from familiarity or affection (Valluvar gives this quality its own chapter, 58, where it is praised in private life, which is why it has to be ruled out here); இறைபுரிந்து is glossed by Parimelazhagar as holding to impartiality (இறை = நடுவுநிலைமை), though some modern readers take இறை as ‘the ruler’ and the phrase as ‘the king, wishing it’; and தேர்ந்து செய்வது means deciding with those learned in the law books and then giving the fitting penalty. யார்மாட்டும் (‘with anyone at all’) governs the whole sequence, so a kinsman gets no exemption. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah follow this procedural reading; Kalaignar compresses it to ‘not leaning to either side’. Parimelazhagar notes that the chapter follows பொச்சாவாமை (vigilance) and comes before its opposite, கொடுங்கோன்மை (Ch. 56); செங்கோல், the ‘straight sceptre’, is the standard Tamil metonym for just rule. ytamizh and Thirukkural.net give the same text.

tamil:
வானோக்கி வாழும் உலகெல்லாம் மன்னவன்
கோல்நோக்கி வாழுங் குடி.
transliteration:
Vaanokki Vaazhum Ulakellaam Mannavan
Kolnokki Vaazhung Kuti.
current_meaning: Every living thing on earth looks to the sky for rain, and in the same way the people of a land look to their king’s sceptre, meaning his just rule, in order to live.
elementary_explanation: Plants in a garden wait for rain, and without it they dry up. The people of a country are a bit like that garden: they are waiting for their leaders to be fair and kind. When the leader rules well, it is like a good rain, and everyone grows.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on an exact parallel: வான் நோக்கி வாழும் உலகு (the world that lives looking to the sky) matches கோல் நோக்கி வாழும் குடி (the citizenry that lives looking to the sceptre). As commentators note, வான் here stands for rain by metonymy, which echoes the opening chapter on rain (வான்சிறப்பு, Ch. 2), where rain sustains all life. Parimelazhagar reads உலகெல்லாம் as ‘all living beings’ and குடி as the settled subjects of the kingdom. Just as he reads கோல் throughout the chapter, the sceptre means just rule, not simply power. Varadarasan and Pappaiah keep the rain comparison; Kalaignar makes it ‘good government is as necessary to citizens as rain is to living things’. The comparison already hints at 545 and 559 (in the next chapter), where just rule and rainfall are causally linked. Both sources agree on the text; வாழுங் is the sandhi form of வாழும் before குடி.

tamil:
அந்தணர் நூற்கும் அறத்திற்கும் ஆதியாய்
நின்றது மன்னவன் கோல்.
transliteration:
Andhanar Noorkum Araththirkum Aadhiyaai
Nindradhu Mannavan Kol.
current_meaning: The king’s sceptre is the foundation that keeps both the scriptures of the sages and the dharma they teach standing.
elementary_explanation: Think of a town library. The books are wonderful, but if nobody keeps the doors safe and the roof mended, the books get ruined and people stop reading. A fair ruler is like the person who keeps the library safe, so that good teachings and good behaviour can last.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar takes அந்தணர் நூல் as the Vedas and அறம் as the dharma they lay down, and he explains ஆதியாய் நின்றது (‘stood as the origin’) causally: if the sceptre fails, the Veda is forgotten and dharma lapses, so the sceptre is their support, not their source in time. Varadarasan follows him (‘the scripture revered by the Brahmins’). Modern commentators widen the terms: Solomon Pappaiah reads அந்தணர் as ‘those who cultivate wisdom’ and நூல் as their books of knowledge, Kalaignar speaks of ‘the books of the virtuous’, and Sivayogi Sivakumar reads அந்தணர் as ‘those who know the end’. The couplet sets out a characteristic Kural view: learning and morality are not self-sustaining; they need a just political order to protect them. Pope’s ‘Learning and virtue of the sages spring / From all-controlling sceptre of the king’ overstates the idea of origin. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
குடிதழீஇக் கோலோச்சும் மாநில மன்னன்
அடிதழீஇ நிற்கும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Kutidhazheeik Kolochchum Maanila Mannan
Atidhazheei Nirkum Ulaku.
current_meaning: The world stays clinging to the feet of the great king who rules while embracing his people.
elementary_explanation: A team captain who looks after every player, helping the slow ones and cheering up the scared ones, ends up with a team that would follow her anywhere. People hold on to a leader who holds on to them first.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a chiasmus of the verb தழுவு (embrace), used twice in the lengthened form தழீஇ: the king embraces the people (குடி தழீஇ), and the world embraces his feet (அடி தழீஇ). The long vowel (இசைநிறை அளபெடை) fills out the metre and gives the word emphasis. கோல் ஓச்சுதல், ‘wielding the sceptre’, is the idiom for ruling. Parimelazhagar explains ‘embracing the subjects’ as protecting them with love and learning what they lack; ‘clinging to his feet’ means the world will not leave him, so his kingdom stands firm. Varadarasan: ‘the world holds fast to the feet of the king who rules embracing his people with love’. Pappaiah turns it into people living ‘around the feet’ of such a ruler, and Kalaignar has the whole earth honouring the footsteps of a good government. In சுற்றந்தழால் (Ch. 53) Valluvar used the same verb for embracing kin; here the embrace is extended to the whole people. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
இயல்புளிக் கோலோச்சும் மன்னவன் நாட்ட
பெயலும் விளையுளும் தொக்கு.
transliteration:
Iyalpulik Kolochchum Mannavan Naatta
Peyalum Vilaiyulum Thokku.
current_meaning: In the land of a king who rules by the proper law, seasonal rain and rich harvests are found together.
elementary_explanation: When a family shares fairly and nobody grabs, dinner time is happy and there is enough for everyone. The old Tamil poets believed a whole country works that way: when the ruler is fair, even the rain and the crops seem to join in.
university_explanation: இயல்புளி is இயல்பு with the instrumental ending உளி (= ஆல்), ‘by the proper nature/way’. Parimelazhagar glosses it as ruling according to the method laid down in the books of statecraft (நீதிநூல்), and Varadarasan (‘நீதி முறைப்படி’) and Pappaiah (‘அரச நீதிநூல்கள் கூறியபடி’) follow him. நாட்ட is a genitive plural predicate, ‘belong to his land’. பெயல் is seasonal rainfall and விளையுள் the abundant yield. The final தொக்கு (having gathered together) means the two are always found together there. Behind the couplet lies a belief found across ancient cultures, that the king’s righteousness governs the fertility of the land. Valluvar states the negative in the next chapter: முறைகோடி மன்னவன் செய்யின் உறைகோடி ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல் (559). Kalaignar reads it as a simile, that just government is like timely rain bringing a good harvest, which softens the causal claim. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
வேலன்று வென்றி தருவது மன்னவன்
கோலதூஉங் கோடா தெனின்.
transliteration:
Velandru Vendri Tharuvadhu Mannavan
Koladhooung Kotaa Thenin.
current_meaning: It is not the spear that brings a king victory but his sceptre, provided that the sceptre does not bend.
elementary_explanation: A kid who wins a game by cheating doesn’t really win, because soon nobody wants to play with him. A kid who plays fair keeps her friends and keeps winning. For a ruler too, being fair is stronger than being scary.
university_explanation: The couplet sets வேல் (spear, the emblem of military force) against கோல் (sceptre, the emblem of justice), two words that differ by a single consonant. அதூஉம், the lengthened form of அதுவும் (‘that too’, with அளபெடை), adds a condition: the sceptre gives victory only if it too does not bend (கோடாது எனின்). The verb கோடு, ‘to bend, be crooked’, is the root of கொடுங்கோல் (tyranny, Ch. 56). Parimelazhagar explains that the spear wins only because the subjects stand loyally with a just king, so victory really comes from the sceptre and the spear is its instrument. Varadarasan and Pappaiah agree; Kalaignar makes the contrast explicit: not the spear that fells enemies, but the unbending sceptre that lets the people live. The point anticipates the chapters on the army (77–78), which treat military strength as dependent on the loyalty that just rule creates. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
இறைகாக்கும் வையகம் எல்லாம் அவனை
முறைகாக்கும் முட்டாச் செயின்.
transliteration:
Iraikaakkum Vaiyakam Ellaam Avanai
Muraikaakkum Muttaach Cheyin.
current_meaning: The king guards the whole world, and justice guards the king, as long as he administers it without fail.
elementary_explanation: If you always tell the truth and treat your friends fairly, then when someone spreads a nasty rumour about you, your friends stand up for you. Your fairness becomes your shield. It works the same way for rulers.
university_explanation: The two halves mirror each other with the verb காக்கும் (guards): இறை காக்கும் வையகம் எல்லாம் (the lord guards the whole world) and அவனை முறை காக்கும் (justice guards him). The condition முட்டாச் செயின், ‘if he does it without lapse’ (முட்டு = obstruction, failure), is the hinge. Parimelazhagar explains that the merit of just rule protects the king from harm that would otherwise come to him; Varadarasan: ‘if he rules without harming justice, that justice itself protects him’. Pappaiah reads முட்டா as qualifying முறை, i.e. ‘his flawless, upright rule protects him’. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads the condition oddly (‘even if they err’), which the grammar does not support. The idea is the political counterpart of the Aram principle that dharma protects those who protect it; compare Manu’s ‘dharmo rakṣati rakṣitaḥ’. Both sources give the same text.

tamil:
எண்பதத்தான் ஓரா முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்
தண்பதத்தான் தானே கெடும்.
transliteration:
Enpadhaththaan Oraa Muraiseyyaa Mannavan
Thanpadhaththaan Thaane Ketum.
current_meaning: A king whom his people cannot easily reach, who does not look into their complaints and give justice, sinks low and perishes by his own doing, even without an enemy.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a class monitor who locks herself away and never listens when kids come to her with a problem. Problems pile up, everyone gets upset, and soon nobody trusts her. She didn’t need an enemy to lose her job. She lost it all by herself.
university_explanation: எண்பதம் means ‘easy access’ (எண் = easy, பதம் = occasion or audience; Varadarasan: எளிய செவ்வி); தண்பதம் means a ‘low state’ (Parimelazhagar: தாழ்ந்த நிலை). The two rhyming compounds frame the couplet. Commentators take the negation of ஓரா (not examining) and முறைசெய்யா (not doing justice) as extending back over எண்பதத்தான், so the king is one who is not accessible, does not investigate, and does not give justice; Pope accordingly renders ‘Hard of access, nought searching out’. Pappaiah keeps the positive reading grammatically but gives the same sense. தானே கெடும் (‘perishes of himself’) is taken by Parimelazhagar and Varadarasan to mean ‘even without enemies’ (பகைவரில்லாமலும்): neglect of justice is self-destruction. Kalaignar departs and reads எண்பதம் as pomp or display. The couplet links accessibility to justice, a theme taken up again in வெருவந்தசெய்யாமை (Ch. 57). The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
குடிபுறங் காத்தோம்பிக் குற்றம் கடிதல்
வடுவன்று வேந்தன் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Kutipurang Kaaththompik Kutram Katidhal
Vatuvandru Vendhan Thozhil.
current_meaning: Guarding the people from outside harm, caring for them, and curbing crime by punishment is no blemish on a king; it is his proper work.
elementary_explanation: A lifeguard who blows her whistle at kids running by the pool isn’t being mean. It is her job, keeping everyone safe. A fair ruler who stops people from doing wrong is doing the same kind of job.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar separates two kinds of protection: புறம் காத்து, guarding the people from others (enemies, robbers, grasping officials), and ஓம்பி, protecting them from himself (for example, by not over-taxing). Only then comes குற்றம் கடிதல், removing crime by fitting punishment. வடு அன்று (‘not a scar or blemish’) answers an implied objection that punishment, as a form of harm, conflicts with the ethic of non-injury taught in the Aram section (e.g. Ch. 32–33); வேந்தன் தொழில் (‘the king’s work’) makes it a duty of office. Varadarasan follows Parimelazhagar closely. Pappaiah reads குற்றம் as the people’s grievances (குறைகள்), which shifts the emphasis from punishment to redress. Kalaignar adds that the ruler should punish whoever the offender is, without fearing reproach. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads புறம் as ‘beyond the borders’. The couplet prepares for the harsher 550. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
கொலையிற் கொடியாரை வேந்தொறுத்தல் பைங்கூழ்
களைகட் டதனொடு நேர்.
transliteration:
Kolaiyir Kotiyaarai Vendhoruththal Paingoozh
Kalaikat Tadhanotu Ner.
current_meaning: For a king to punish violent criminals with death is like a farmer pulling up weeds to save the green crop.
elementary_explanation: A gardener pulls out weeds not because she hates plants but because the weeds would choke the vegetables. The Kural says a ruler must stop people who seriously hurt others, so that everyone else can grow up safe. (Grown-ups still argue about how harsh such punishments should be.)
university_explanation: The final couplet puts the chapter’s argument about punishment in an agricultural image: பைங்கூழ் is the young green crop, and களை கட்டல் is weeding. The phrase கொலையிற் கொடியாரை is read in two ways. Varadarasan and Pappaiah take கொலையின் as instrumental, so the king punishes the cruel ‘by death’ (கொலைத்தண்டனையால்). Kalaignar takes it as the offence, so the cruel are ‘those who commit murder and similar cruelties’. Parimelazhagar’s commentary follows the first line of reading and presents capital punishment as the protection of the good, just as the weed is removed for the crop’s sake. Commentators note the tension with the Aram section’s உயிர் கொல்லாமை (not killing, Ch. 33). The usual resolution is that Aram states the individual’s ethic while Porul states the king’s duty. Modern readers such as Kalaignar keep the metaphor but stress that it applies to hardened offenders, not the ordinary wrongdoer. The next chapter, Tyranny, reverses the image. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
கொலைமேற்கொண் டாரிற் கொடிதே அலைமேற்கொண்டு
அல்லவை செய்தொழுகும் வேந்து.
transliteration:
Kolaimerkon daarir kodithe alaimerkondu
Allavai seythozhukum vendhu.
current_meaning: A king who makes a practice of harassing his people and keeps doing what is unjust is crueler than someone whose trade is murder.
elementary_explanation: Picture a playground bully who knocks you over once, and then picture a class monitor who is supposed to look after everyone but pushes kids around every single day. The monitor is worse, because the hurt never stops and the one person meant to protect you is the one hurting you. Valluvar says a cruel king is like that monitor, only much bigger.
university_explanation: The chapter is the mirror image of the preceding one, செங்கோன்மை (the straight sceptre, ch. 55): கொடுங்கோல் is the ‘bent’ rod of a ruler who governs by oppression. The key word அலை means harassing or tormenting, and Parimelazhagar glosses அலைமேற்கொண்டு as taking up, out of covetousness for wealth (பொருள்வெஃகி), the business of harassing the subjects. His reason for the comparison is that the murderer’s harm lasts a moment, whereas the tyrant’s is lifelong, so ‘harassment is crueller than killing’. He also notes the grammatical point that வேந்து, a neuter-class noun, is used here of a person (திணை/பால் மயக்கம்). Manakkudavar gives substantially the same reading, while Solomon Pappaiah stresses greed for the people’s property. The text is uniform across ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com; the older continuous text on thirukkural-thamizh.org shows the unsplit sandhi forms யலைமேற்கொண் / டல்லவை.

tamil:
வேலொடு நின்றான் இடுவென் றதுபோலும்
கோலொடு நின்றான் இரவு.
transliteration:
Velodu nindraan iduven rathupolum
Kolodu nindraan iravu.
current_meaning: When a ruler who holds the sceptre asks his subjects for money, it is like a robber standing with a spear on a lonely road and saying ‘Hand it over’.
elementary_explanation: If a big kid holding a stick says ‘Can I please have your lunch?’, it isn’t really a question, because you know what happens if you say no. Valluvar says that when a king with power over you ‘asks’ for extra money, it is the same as a robber demanding it.
university_explanation: The image is of the solitary highwayman (வேலொடு நின்றான்) and the king ‘standing with the rod’ (கோலொடு நின்றான்), the rod here meaning the power to punish (ஒறுத்தல் தொழில்). Parimelazhagar draws two inferences: ‘standing with a spear’ implies the robber is alone on a deserted road, and the word இரவு (begging, request) shows that what the king asks for is not the lawful revenue (இறைப்பொருள் அன்மை). Because the king’s request carries an unspoken threat to punish anyone who refuses, even ‘asking’ becomes tyranny; he adds that kurals 551-552 together state the fault of tyranny itself. Manakkudavar reads கோலொடு நிற்றல் as standing in the posture of one who administers justice, and adds that even a voluntary-seeming levy above the fixed dues is like robbery on the road. Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take the couplet as a comment on extortionate taxation. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

tamil:
நாடொறும் நாடி முறைசெய்யா மன்னவன்
நாடொறும் நாடு கெடும்.
transliteration:
Naadorum naadi muraiseyyaa mannavan
Naadorum naadu kedum.
current_meaning: A king who does not look into wrongs every day and give justice will see his country decline a little more every day.
elementary_explanation: If you never look after a garden, weeds creep in a little each day until the flowers are gone. A king who doesn’t check every day for unfair things happening, and fix them, lets his whole country slowly go to ruin in the same way.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on நாள் / நாடு: நாடொறும் (daily, from நாள் + தொறும்) and நாடி (examining, from நாடு-தல்), then நாடு (country). Parimelazhagar glosses: the king who does not daily examine the wrongs occurring in his land and render fitting justice will daily ‘lose’ his country. He explains that since the country is a limb (உறுப்பு) of the king, the verb ‘perish’ is attributed to him, and that ‘losing’ here means failing to enjoy its fruits (பயன் எய்தாமை). He records an alternative construal, ‘the king’s country perishes daily’ (மன்னவன் நாடு நாள்தொறும் கெடும்), which Manakkudavar and Kalaignar adopt. For the first word, thirukkural.com prints the unassimilated form நாள்தொறும், while ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give the sandhi form நாடொறும்.

tamil:
கூழுங் குடியும் ஒருங்கிழக்கும் கோல்கோடிச்
சூழாது செய்யும் அரசு.
transliteration:
Koozhung kudiyum orungizhakkum kolkodich
Choozhaathu seyyum arasu.
current_meaning: A king who bends justice and acts without thinking about the consequences loses both his wealth and his people at once.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a lemonade stand owner who cheats customers without thinking ahead. Soon the customers stop coming, and with them goes the money. Valluvar says a careless, unfair king loses his treasure and his people together, because the people are where the treasure comes from.
university_explanation: கூழ் (literally gruel or food) stands for wealth, and குடி for the subjects. Parimelazhagar makes the pairing precise: கூழ் is the wealth already amassed, and குடி is the people who are the source of wealth yet to be earned, so the tyrant loses past and future income together. சூழாது means ‘without deliberating’ on what will follow, and கோல்கோடி means ‘bending the sceptre’; he notes கோடி stands for the infinitive கோட. He adds that the next couplet gives the cause of losing wealth already amassed. Manakkudavar marks this couplet as stating the fault that comes from acting without deliberation. Kalaignar reads குடி more loosely as ‘the people’s esteem’. The text is the same across the sources consulted, and Pope’s rendering ‘who counsel doth refuse’ follows the sense of சூழாது.

tamil:
அல்லற்பட்டு ஆற்றாது அழுதகண் ணீரன்றே
செல்வத்தைத் தேய்க்கும் படை.
transliteration:
Allarpattu aatraathu azhuthakan neerandre
Selvaththaith theykkum padai.
current_meaning: The tears of people who suffer and cannot bear it any longer are the weapon that wears away an oppressive king’s wealth.
elementary_explanation: Water dripping on a stone for a long, long time can wear a hole right through it. Valluvar says the tears of people treated unfairly are like that water: drop by drop, they wear away the riches of the ruler who made them cry.
university_explanation: அல்லல் is distress, ஆற்றாது ‘unable to bear it’, and படை ‘army’ or ‘weapon’. The verb தேய்க்கும் (wears away, grinds down) has led translators to render படை as a file or saw (Pope has ‘sharp instruments’, and the prose translation ‘a saw’). Parimelazhagar calls the figure ஏகதேச உருவகம் (partial metaphor): Valluvar does not say ‘the tree of wealth’, but the verb implies it. He explains that the destructive work really done by the sin of causing suffering is credited to the tears that are its sign, ‘because nothing is crueller than those tears’, and that the sense is that the wealth wastes away quickly. He groups kurals 553-556 as stating the evils that befall the tyrant himself. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

tamil:
மன்னர்க்கு மன்னுதல் செங்கோன்மை அஃதின்றேல்
மன்னாவாம் மன்னர்க் கொளி.
transliteration:
Mannarkku mannuthal sengonmai akhthindrel
Mannaavaam mannark koli.
current_meaning: Just rule is what makes a king’s fame last; without it, his glory will not endure.
elementary_explanation: A trophy you won by cheating doesn’t feel like yours, and people stop cheering once they find out. Valluvar says a king’s glory is like that: only fair, honest rule keeps it shining, and without fairness it fades away.
university_explanation: The couplet repeats the root மன்- ‘to endure’ for effect: மன்னர் (kings), மன்னுதல் (enduring) and மன்னா (will not endure). ஒளி (light, lustre) means renown. Parimelazhagar supplies the instrumental case lost by elision: ‘kings’ fame endures by the straight sceptre’. He cites Nāṉmaṇikkaṭikai 17 (‘if you wish to endure in this world, plant fame’) to show that fame is what makes a person endure. He explains the plural (ஒளி taken as many forms of fame, from victory, generosity and so on) and concludes that if their fame does not last, the kings themselves do not last. Some continuous-text editions read the sandhi form அஃதின்றேன் and மன்னாவா மன்னர்க் for அஃதின்றேல் மன்னாவாம். Manakkudavar puts this couplet first in the ‘faults’ series, taking the loss of glory as the first penalty of misrule.

tamil:
துளியின்மை ஞாலத்திற்கு எற்றற்றே வேந்தன்
அளியின்மை வாழும் உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Thuliyinmai gnaalaththirku etratre vendhan
Aliyinmai vaazhum uyirkku.
current_meaning: What drought is to the world, a king’s lack of kindness is to the people who live under him.
elementary_explanation: When it doesn’t rain for a long time, plants wilt, rivers shrink, and animals go thirsty. A king without kindness makes his people wilt in just the same way, because his care is like rain to them.
university_explanation: துளி (a drop) stands for rain by synecdoche. Parimelazhagar says the word was chosen because a drop is the most telling part of rain. அளி means gracious, tender care, and உயிர் (life, living beings) here stands for the subjects. The construction எற்று… அற்றே (‘of what kind…? just so’) makes a rhetorical comparison. Parimelazhagar notes that this couplet puts negatively what kural 542 had said positively: the whole world lives looking to the sky for rain, and the subjects look to the king’s sceptre. He groups kurals 557-558 as stating the evils that fall on those who live in the tyrant’s land. Solomon Pappaiah reads அளி more broadly as ‘righteous governance’. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

tamil:
இன்மையின் இன்னாது உடைமை முறைசெய்யா
மன்னவன் கோற்கீழ்ப் படின்.
transliteration:
Inmaiyin innaathu udaimai muraiseyyaa
Mannavan korkeezhp padin.
current_meaning: Under the sceptre of an unjust king, having wealth brings more misery than having nothing.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a class where a mean monitor takes the best toy from anyone who brings one. Soon, the kids who bring nice toys are the most worried ones. Valluvar says that under a greedy king, being rich becomes more dangerous than being poor.
university_explanation: The paradox turns on இன்மை (having nothing) and உடைமை (possessing). Parimelazhagar explains it by describing what the covetous king does: those who own property are the ones who suffer seizures, torture and binding ‘till the hands ache’ (கைந்நோவ யாப்புண்டல்), so under such a ruler wealth is worse than poverty. He applies it to everyone (யாவர்க்கும்), not just the rich, and groups kurals 557-558 as stating the evils that fall on those who live in the tyrant’s land. Manakkudavar agrees (‘even the wealthy suffer’) and counts 557-559 as the evils of failing to do justice. கோற்கீழ்ப் படின் means ‘if one falls under the sceptre’. The text is the same across the sources consulted.

tamil:
முறைகோடி மன்னவன் செய்யின் உறைகோடி
ஒல்லாது வானம் பெயல்.
transliteration:
Muraikodi mannavan seyyin uraikodi
Ollaathu vaanam peyal.
current_meaning: If a king rules against justice, the seasons go wrong and the sky will not send its rain.
elementary_explanation: Think of a team captain who cheats. Soon nobody plays well, the whole game falls apart, and it feels as if even luck has left. The old poets said that when a king is unfair, even the rain stops coming on time.
university_explanation: The couplet repeats கோடி (bending): the king ‘bends’ justice (முறைகோடி) and the rain ‘bends’ from its season (உறைகோடி). Parimelazhagar notes that both forms stand for the infinitive கோட, glosses உறைகோடுதல் as ‘failing to rain at the time for rain’, and says the cause is given in the next couplet. Classical commentators take this as a real cosmic link between royal righteousness and the monsoon, a belief widespread in Indian thought. Kalaignar instead reads உறை as reservoirs and rain-storage works that fall to ruin under misrule, so the rain cannot be stored and used. The text is the same across the sources consulted, apart from sandhi spacing in the older continuous text (செய்யி னுறைகோடி யொல்லாது).

tamil:
ஆபயன் குன்றும் அறுதொழிலோர் நூல்மறப்பர்
காவலன் காவான் எனின்.
transliteration:
Aapayan kundrum aruthozhilor noolmarappar
Kaavalan kaavaan enin.
current_meaning: If the guardian of the land fails to protect it, the cows give less milk and the learned men of the six duties forget their scriptures.
elementary_explanation: If a school has no one looking after it, the lunch kitchen stops working and the teachers stop teaching. Soon both food and learning are gone. Valluvar says that when a king doesn’t protect his land, food (milk from cows) and learning (the old books) both start to fade.
university_explanation: ஆபயன் is ‘the yield of the cow’ (ஆ, cow, and பயன், fruit), meaning milk and its products. அறுதொழிலோர் are ‘those of the six duties’, which Parimelazhagar lists as the Brahmin’s six duties: studying, teaching, sacrificing, officiating at sacrifice, giving and receiving (ஓதல், ஓதுவித்தல், வேட்டல், வேட்பித்தல், ஈதல், ஏற்றல்). He ties the couplet to 559: without milk there is no oblation (அவி), without recitation there are no mantras, so sacrifice stops, and so the rain fails. He groups 559-560 as the evils that befall the tyrant’s land. Modern commentators widen the reference: Solomon Pappaiah reads ‘the wise’ (ஞானியர்), and Kalaignar and Sivayogi Sivakumar read ‘productive work and the major occupations decline’. The older continuous text has the sandhi form நூன்மறப்பர்.

tamil:
தக்காங்கு நாடித் தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால்
ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுப்பது வேந்து.
transliteration:
Thakkaangu naadith thalaichchellaa vannaththaal
Oththaangu oruppadhu vaendhu.
current_meaning: A true king first investigates a wrong fairly and thoroughly, and then punishes it in a measure that fits the offence, so that it is not repeated.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a teacher who finds a broken window. A good teacher first finds out calmly who did it and why, and then gives a fair consequence, not too big and not too small, so it won't happen again. This kural says a good ruler works the same way: find out the truth first, then correct fairly.
university_explanation: The chapter title வெருவந்த செய்யாமை means ‘not doing things that cause dread (veru)’, and Valluvar opens it not by forbidding punishment but by defining its right form. Three steps are packed into the couplet: தக்காங்கு நாடி (investigating as is fitting, i.e., impartially), ஒத்தாங்கு ஒறுத்தல் (punishing in a measure that matches the offence), and the purpose clause தலைச்செல்லா வண்ணத்தால் (so that the wrong does not advance or recur). The traditional commentators, with Parimelazhagar at their head, read this as the positive standard against which the tyranny of the previous chapter (கொடுங்கோன்மை, ch. 56) is measured, and modern glosses (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) all stress neutrality in inquiry and proportion in penalty. The definition-style ending ‘… வேந்து’ (‘that is a king’) makes proportionate justice constitutive of kingship itself. Text agrees across ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the latter printing the older sandhi-joined form (வண்ணத்தா / லொத்தாங் கொறுப்பது) with no change in wording.

tamil:
கடிதோச்சி மெல்ல எறிக நெடிதாக்கம்
நீங்காமை வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Kadidhoachchi mella eriga nedidhaakkam
Neengaamai vaendu bavar.
current_meaning: Rulers who want their prosperity to last long should raise the rod sternly but let it fall gently: firm in warning, mild in the actual penalty.
elementary_explanation: Think of a parent who says in a serious voice, ‘If you do that again, there will be no TV for a month!’, but when it happens, takes away TV for just one evening. The warning is strong, the punishment is gentle. The kural says leaders who do this keep their people’s trust for a long time.
university_explanation: The image is of a raised stick: கடிது ஓச்சி (lift it high, severely) but மெல்ல எறிக (bring it down softly). The classical commentary, followed by Mu. Varadarasanar, reads this as appearing to proceed with great severity while in fact not exceeding due measure, while Kalaignar’s modern gloss separates the stages as stern reproof but mild punishment. The reward named is நெடிது ஆக்கம் நீங்காமை, prosperity that does not depart for a long time, so the couplet argues from prudence as much as from mercy. Pope’s ‘raise the rod with brow severe, but let it gently fall’ has become the standard English rendering. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi form ‘மெல்ல வெறிக’, which is the same words as ‘மெல்ல எறிக’.

tamil:
வெருவந்த செய்தொழுகும் வெங்கோல னாயின்
ஒருவந்தம் ஒல்லைக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Veruvandha seydhozhugum vengoalan aayin
Oruvandham ollaik kedum.
current_meaning: A cruel-sceptred king who habitually does things that fill his people with dread will certainly and swiftly be ruined.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a team captain who yells and scares everyone all the time. Soon nobody wants to play for them, and the team falls apart. The kural says a ruler who keeps people frightened will quickly lose everything.
university_explanation: This couplet supplies the chapter’s title phrase: வெருவந்த செய்து ஒழுகும் describes a ruler whose habitual conduct (ஒழுகுதல், ongoing practice) is to do dread-inducing things. வெங்கோலன், the ‘hot’ or cruel sceptre, is the opposite of the செங்கோல் (straight sceptre) of chapter 55. ஒருவந்தம் means ‘certainly, without doubt’ and ஒல்லை ‘quickly’, so the prediction is doubly emphatic: sure and soon. Commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) agree in glossing ‘veru’ as the fear felt by the subjects (குடிகள் அஞ்சும்படி). The couplet is read identically in both sources consulted.

tamil:
இறைகடியன் என்றுரைக்கும் இன்னாச்சொல் வேந்தன்
உறைகடுகி ஒல்லைக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Iraikadiyan endruraikkum innaachchol vaendhan
Uraikadugi ollaik kedum.
current_meaning: A king who earns the bitter name ‘our ruler is cruel’ from his people will have his span cut short and will quickly perish.
elementary_explanation: If everyone at school whispers ‘the new class monitor is mean,’ that monitor won’t be monitor for long. The kural says when a whole country calls its king cruel, his time is almost up.
university_explanation: The couplet turns from the ruler’s acts to the people’s verdict: இறை கடியன் (‘the lord is harsh’) is the இன்னாச் சொல், the painful word, that the subjects speak. The ruler is thus defined by his reputation, and public opinion becomes a political force. உறை கடுகி is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘his lifespan shrinking’ (ஆயுள் குறைந்து), while Pappaiah reads it as the term of his rule contracting; both readings fit, and Pope’s ‘his age shall dwindle’ follows the first. ஒல்லைக் கெடும் repeats the ‘swiftly perishes’ of 563, binding the two couplets together. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
அருஞ்செவ்வி இன்னா முகத்தான் பெருஞ்செல்வம்
பேஎய்கண் டன்னது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Arunjevvi innaa mugaththaan perunjelvam
Paeey kandannadhu udaiththu.
current_meaning: The vast wealth of a ruler who is hard to see and who greets people with a harsh face is like treasure guarded by a demon: frightening and of no use to anyone.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a huge toy box that belongs to someone who never opens the door and scowls at everyone who knocks. Nobody gets to play with the toys, so it’s as if a monster were sitting on them. The kural says a leader who can’t be reached and always frowns makes his riches useless.
university_explanation: Two faults are named: அருஞ்செவ்வி, rare or difficult audience (செவ்வி = an opportune moment of access), and இன்னா முகம், a disagreeable countenance. The simile பேஎய் கண்டு அன்னது is read in the commentarial tradition as wealth that a pēy (demon, ghoul) has seen or seized: it exists but inspires only fear and benefits no one, which is why Pope renders ‘blasted by demon’s glance’ and Pappaiah ‘held by a bhūta’. The couplet widens the chapter’s idea of dread from punishment to everyday demeanour: an unapproachable, scowling ruler terrifies without lifting a rod. The spelling பேஎய் preserves the classical alapedai (vowel prolongation) for metre, and both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
கடுஞ்சொல்லன் கண்ணிலன் ஆயின் நெடுஞ்செல்வம்
நீடின்றி ஆங்கே கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kadunjollan kannilan aayin nedunjelvam
Needindri aangae kedum.
current_meaning: If a ruler is harsh in speech and has no kindly regard for others, his great wealth will not last; it will perish then and there.
elementary_explanation: A shopkeeper who is rude and never smiles at customers soon has an empty shop, no matter how many goods are on the shelves. The kural says a leader with harsh words and no kindness loses even great riches very quickly.
university_explanation: கடுஞ்சொல்லன் is one given to harsh words, and கண்ணிலன், literally ‘eyeless’, means lacking kaṇṇōṭṭam, the gracious, considerate regard that is the subject of the very next chapter (58, கண்ணோட்டம்). The couplet thus bridges two chapters: without kindly regard, even நெடுஞ்செல்வம் (vast, long-accumulated wealth) perishes நீடின்றி ஆங்கே, without delay, on the spot. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses கண்ணிலன் as கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாதவன் and Pappaiah as lacking முகதாட்சண்யம் (considerateness), while Kalaignar renders it as a ‘merciless heart’. The contrast நெடும் (long) and நீடு இன்றி (without lasting) is a deliberate verbal play. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
கடுமொழியும் கையிகந்த தண்டமும் வேந்தன்
அடுமுரண் தேய்க்கும் அரம்.
transliteration:
Kadumozhiyum kaiyigandha thandamum vaendhan
Adumuran thaeykkum aram.
current_meaning: Harsh words and punishments that exceed all measure are a file that slowly wears away a king’s power to defeat his enemies.
elementary_explanation: A metal file rubs a little bit off a key every time you use it, until one day the key no longer works. The kural says that every cruel word and every too-big punishment rubs away a little of a leader’s strength, until it is gone.
university_explanation: கையிகந்த தண்டம் is punishment that has ‘gone beyond the hand’, exceeding its proper limit (Mu. Varadarasanar: முறைகடந்த தண்டனை). அடுமுரண் is the destroying strength, the capacity to crush enemies, and அரம் is a file, so the metaphor is of gradual erosion rather than sudden collapse, complementing the ‘swift ruin’ of 563–566. The couplet echoes 566 (harsh words) and 561 (proportionate punishment), making excess, not punishment itself, the target. The word தண்டம் (Sanskrit daṇḍa) links Valluvar to the wider Indian daṇḍanīti tradition of measured punishment. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi form ‘அடுமுரண் டேய்க்கு மரம்’, identical in wording.

tamil:
இனத்தாற்றி எண்ணாத வேந்தன் சினத்தாற்றிச்
சீறிற் சிறுகும் திரு.
transliteration:
Inaththaatri ennaadha vaendhan sinaththaatrich
Seeril sirugum thiru.
current_meaning: A king who does not think matters through with his counsellors, and then gives way to anger and lashes out at them, will see his fortune shrink.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a group leader who never asks the team for ideas, and then, when the project goes wrong, shouts at everyone. The team stops helping, and things get worse and worse. The kural says a leader who skips advice and then explodes in anger loses what they have.
university_explanation: The couplet is syntactically compact and has two established readings. Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah take இனத்து ஆற்றி எண்ணாத as ‘not deliberating together with his circle (ministers)’, so the fault is failure to consult followed by angry outbursts; Pope, following the older commentary, reads it as handing affairs to ministers without himself reflecting, and then raging at them when things fail. On either reading the pattern is the same: neglect of counsel, then சினத்து ஆற்றி சீறுதல், being carried along by anger and flaring at subordinates. The result is that திரு (Śrī, royal fortune) சிறுகும், dwindles. Here ‘dread’ is directed at the king’s own ministers, extending the chapter’s concern from subjects to the inner court. The text is the same in both sources.

tamil:
செருவந்த போழ்திற் சிறைசெய்யா வேந்தன்
வெருவந்து வெய்து கெடும்.
transliteration:
Seruvandha poazhdhil siraiseyyaa vaendhan
Veruvandhu veydhu kedum.
current_meaning: A king who has not prepared a place of defence beforehand will, when war arrives, be seized with fear and quickly perish.
elementary_explanation: If you never build a shelter and a big storm comes, you get frightened and soaked. The kural says a ruler who doesn’t prepare protection in peaceful times panics and falls when trouble arrives.
university_explanation: சிறை here means a protective barrier or fortification (Mu. Varadarasanar: அரண்), not ‘prison’ in the modern sense; the couplet is about defence made ready before செரு (battle) arrives. The striking reversal is in வெருவந்து: the very dread (veru) the tyrant inflicted on others now falls on him, so the chapter’s key word turns back on its source. Commentators connect this to the preceding couplets: a king who has alienated his people through fear and cruelty lacks the human ‘fortress’ of their loyalty when danger comes, which is why this apparently military verse belongs in a chapter on not ruling by terror. வெய்து கெடும் means ‘perishes swiftly/painfully’. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
கல்லார்ப் பிணிக்கும் கடுங்கோல் அதுவல்லது
இல்லை நிலக்குப் பொறை.
transliteration:
Kallaarp pinikkum kadungoal adhuvalladhu
Illai nilakkup porai.
current_meaning: A harsh sceptre that binds ignorant, unlearned men to itself as its helpers is the heaviest burden the earth has to bear; there is none greater.
elementary_explanation: Picture a bully who gathers other kids who don’t know right from wrong to help him push everyone around. That gang makes the whole playground miserable. The kural says a cruel ruler with foolish helpers is the heaviest weight the world has to carry.
university_explanation: The closing couplet names the social mechanism of tyranny: கடுங்கோல் (the harsh sceptre) பிணிக்கும் (binds, attaches) கல்லார் (the unlearned) to itself, meaning it draws in and relies on men without learning or moral training to carry out its will. The traditional commentary, followed by Mu. Varadarasanar, Kalaignar, and Pope (‘Tyrants with fools their counsels share’), reads it this way; Pappaiah’s gloss instead stresses a regime that punishes so as to terrify, propped up by those who have not studied the books of justice. பொறை means a load or burden, and the idea of the earth (நிலம்) groaning under wicked rulers is widespread in Indian thought. The couplet ties back to chapter 41 (கல்லாமை, lack of learning) and closes the chapter by showing that terror is never exercised alone. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints the sandhi-joined ‘கடுங்கோ லதுவல்ல தில்லை’, identical in wording.

tamil:
கண்ணோட்டம் என்னும் கழிபெருங் காரிகை
உண்மையான் உண்டிவ் வுலகு.
transliteration:
Kannottam ennum kazhiperung kaarikai
Unmaiyaan undiv vulagu.
current_meaning: The world keeps going only because there exists that surpassingly great beauty called kannottam, a kindly, gracious regard for others.
elementary_explanation: Think of a playground where the big kids notice the little ones and help them up when they fall. That kind look makes the whole playground a happy place. Valluvar says the whole world keeps going because people, especially leaders, look at others kindly like that.
university_explanation: The chapter title கண்ணோட்டம் literally means ‘the running (ஓட்டம்) of the eye (கண்)’, i.e., the eye going out towards another in consideration; Parimelazhagar defines it as the disposition that, on seeing those one is familiar with, cannot bring itself to refuse or hurt them, and he places the chapter in the Arasiyal (royal) section as a quality of the king. The phrase கழிபெருங் காரிகை (‘exceedingly great beauty’) treats benignity as an ornament rather than a duty, a theme picked up again in kural 575. The second line, உண்மையான் உண்டு இவ்வுலகு (‘because of its existence, this world exists’), is a strong ontological claim: social order itself depends on this quality. Modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah) gloss it as ‘looking at a person’s face’ and softening accordingly, while Kalaignar reads it more broadly as love joined with compassion. The text agrees across ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the latter printing the older sandhi-joined form (கண்ணோட்ட மென்னுங் … யுண்மையா னுண்டிவ்) with no change in wording.

tamil:
கண்ணோட்டத் துள்ளது உலகியல் அஃதிலார்
உண்மை நிலக்குப் பொறை.
transliteration:
Kannottath thulladhu ulagiyal aqdhilaar
Unmai nilakkup porai.
current_meaning: All the ordinary business of the world runs on kindly regard; people who lack it merely exist as a burden on the earth.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a class where everyone shares pencils and helps each other. One child never helps anyone and only takes. The class works because of the helpers; the one who never helps just makes things heavier for everyone. Valluvar says people without kindness are like extra weight the earth has to carry.
university_explanation: உலகியல் means ‘the conduct or course of the world’, i.e., everyday social transactions, and Parimelazhagar takes the first line to mean that all such dealings are sustained by kannottam. The second line’s உண்மை (‘existence’, not ‘truth’ here) and பொறை (‘burden’) make a stark judgement: a person without kindly regard contributes nothing and simply weighs on the land, an image the Tamil tradition also uses of the ungrateful and the idle. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both render பொறை as சுமை/பாரம் (load), while Kalaignar stresses the ‘embracing with love’ that such people lack. The couplet thus moves from the cosmic claim of 571 to its negative corollary. ytamizh.com and thirukkural-thamizh.org agree; the latter prints the sandhi-joined form (துள்ள துலகிய லஃதிலா / ருண்மை).

tamil:
பண்என்னாம் பாடற்கு இயைபின்றேல் கண்என்னாம்
கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்.
transliteration:
Pan ennaam paadarku iyaipindrel kan ennaam
Kannottam illaadha kan.
current_meaning: What use is a melody that does not fit the song? Just so, what use is an eye that has no kindly regard in it?
elementary_explanation: If someone plays a happy tune while you sing a sad lullaby, the music doesn’t help at all; it just sounds wrong. Valluvar says eyes are the same: eyes are meant to look kindly, and eyes without kindness are like music that doesn’t match the song.
university_explanation: பண் is the technical term for a melodic mode in Tamil music (roughly comparable to a raga), and இயைபு means ‘concordance’ or ‘fitting together’; the couplet thus draws on the Tamil musical tradition, in which the right pann had to suit the song and its mood. Parimelazhagar explains that just as a pann not matched to its song is useless, an eye not joined to kannottam is useless, so kindness is the eye’s proper ‘accompaniment’. The rhetorical question என்னாம் (‘what will it be?’, i.e., of what use) is repeated to link the two halves. Solomon Pappaiah renders பண் as ராகம், and all four commentaries on ytamizh.com share this reading. thirukkural-thamizh.org has பண்ணென்னாம் … கியைபின்றேற் for ytamizh’s பண்என்னாம் … இயைபின்றேல், which are orthographic and sandhi differences only.

tamil:
உளபோல் முகத்தெவன் செய்யும் அளவினால்
கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்.
transliteration:
Ulapol mugaththevan seyyum alavinaal
Kannottam illaadha kan.
current_meaning: Eyes that lack kindly regard in due measure only seem to be present in the face; beyond that, what good do they do?
elementary_explanation: A doll can have beautiful painted eyes, but they never notice when you are sad. They are just there for decoration. Valluvar says eyes that never look kindly at anyone are like doll’s eyes: they are in the face, but they are not really doing an eye’s job.
university_explanation: உளபோல் (‘as if they exist’) makes the eyes a mere appearance on the face (முகத்து), and எவன் செய்யும் asks what use they serve. The key qualifier is அளவினால் (‘in due measure’): Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar read the kindness required as kannottam within proper limits, i.e., kindness that does not override duty, which anticipates kural 578. Solomon Pappaiah likewise speaks of ‘kannottam within bounds’ (வரம்பிற்கு உட்பட்ட), while Kalaignar reads it as the eyes failing to stir love and pity in the heart. The couplet shares its second line verbatim with 573 (கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லாத கண்), a deliberate repetition that ties the two images together. thirukkural-thamizh.org prints உளபோன் … மளவினாற் (sandhi forms) for ytamizh’s உளபோல் … அளவினால், with no change in wording.

tamil:
கண்ணிற்கு அணிகலம் கண்ணோட்டம் அஃதின்றேல்
புண்ணென்று உணரப் படும்.
transliteration:
Kannirku anigalam kannottam aqdhindrel
Punnendru unarap padum.
current_meaning: Kindly regard is the jewel that adorns the eye; without it the eyes will be seen as nothing more than two sores.
elementary_explanation: People wear necklaces and bracelets to look nice. Valluvar says the nicest thing your eyes can ‘wear’ is kindness. If your eyes are always angry or cold, people will not see pretty eyes at all; they will see something that hurts, like a scrape.
university_explanation: அணிகலம் (‘ornament, jewel’) recalls the காரிகை (‘beauty’) of 571: kannottam is the eye’s jewellery, not merely its function.
