The shocking alternative, புண் (‘wound, sore’), plays on the near-rhyme கண்/புண், and the passive உணரப்படும் (‘will be perceived as’) implies the judgement of others; Solomon Pappaiah specifies ‘by the wise’ (பெரியோரால்), as does the Pope/Drew-style English gloss on ytamizh. Parimelazhagar’s point is that eyes are honoured only because they carry grace; without it they are merely openings in the flesh. This is the couplet the chapter is most remembered for, and its imagery of ornament versus wound is found in later Tamil ethical literature. The two sources agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms கண்ணிற் கணிகலங் … மஃதின்றேற் / புண்ணென் றுணரப்.

tamil:
மண்ணோ டியைந்த மரத்தனையர் கண்ணோ
டியைந்துகண் ணோடா தவர்.
transliteration:
Mannodu iyaindha maraththanaiyar kannodu
iyaindhukan nodaa thavar.
current_meaning: Those who have eyes yet never look kindly on others are like trees rooted in the soil: they have the form but not the feeling.
elementary_explanation: A tree stands in one place and can’t notice when someone near it is crying. Valluvar says a person who has eyes but never looks kindly at others is just like that tree: standing there, but not really caring about anyone.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a careful parallel: மண்ணோடு இயைந்த மரம் (‘a tree joined to the soil’) and கண்ணோடு இயைந்து கண்ணோடாதவர் (‘those who, though joined to eyes, do not let the eye run out [in kindness]’). The verb கண்ணோடு is the root of the chapter’s title, so the line plays on having கண் (eyes) but not doing கண்ணோட்டம். Parimelazhagar is usually cited as noting that trees too were said to have ‘eyes’ (buds or nodes), so that the unkind are no better than eyed trees; this pun is reported in commentary tradition and should be treated with some caution. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses ‘like a tree that has eyes but does not see’, while Solomon Pappaiah stresses that such people move about but are as insensible as a tree fixed in the earth. The two texts agree word for word, with the line break falling inside கண்ணோ / டியைந்து in both.

tamil:
கண்ணோட்டம் இல்லவர் கண்ணிலர் கண்ணுடையார்
கண்ணோட்டம் இன்மையும் இல்.
transliteration:
Kannottam illavar kannilar kannudaiyaar
Kannottam inmaiyum il.
current_meaning: People without kindly regard are really eyeless; and those who truly have eyes are never without kindly regard.
elementary_explanation: Imagine your friend drops their lunch and everyone looks away, but one kid runs over to help. Valluvar would say only that kid truly ‘saw’. Having real eyes means noticing people and caring about them; if you never care, it is as if you have no eyes at all.
university_explanation: The couplet is a chiasmus built on the single word கண்: those without கண்ணோட்டம் are கண்ணிலர் (‘eyeless’), and those who are கண்ணுடையார் (‘possessed of eyes’) are never without கண்ணோட்டம். Parimelazhagar reads it as a definition by convertibility: in the moral sense, having eyes and having kannottam are one and the same thing, so that physical sight without kindness does not count as sight. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah render it almost identically, while Kalaignar reverses the emphasis, saying the eyes of the compassionate alone deserve the name. With 576 it completes a sequence (573-577) that systematically strips the unkind eye of every value. Both sources agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has sandhi forms கண்ணோட்ட மில்லவர் … மின்மையு மில்.

tamil:
கருமம் சிதையாமல் கண்ணோட வல்லார்க்கு
உரிமை உடைத்திவ் வுலகு.
transliteration:
Karumam sidhaiyaamal kannoda vallaarkku
Urimai udaiththiv vulagu.
current_meaning: The world rightfully belongs to those who can show kindly regard without letting their duty be damaged.
elementary_explanation: A good referee is friendly and kind to all the players, but still calls a foul when someone breaks the rules. Valluvar says the best leaders are like that: kind to everyone, but they never let kindness stop them from doing what is right.
university_explanation: கருமம் here means one’s proper task, and for a king Parimelazhagar specifies it as the administration of justice (the ytamizh English gloss adds ‘administration of justice’ in brackets); சிதையாமல் means ‘without letting it be spoiled’. The couplet thus sets a limit on kannottam: kindness toward familiar people must never become favouritism that ruins just government, which explains the அளவினால் (‘in due measure’) of 574. உரிமை உடைத்து இவ்வுலகு (‘this world has rightful ownership [for them]’) promises that such rulers are the world’s natural possessors. Modern commentators generalise the principle to anyone who is compassionate without neglecting their duties (Kalaignar: ‘first in not failing duty and in showering mercy’). Both texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms கருமஞ் சிதையாமற் … வல்லார்க் / குரிமை யுடைத்திவ்.

tamil:
ஒறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பினார் கண்ணும்கண் ணோடிப்
பொறுத்தாற்றும் பண்பே தலை.
transliteration:
Oruththaatrum panbinaar kannum kannodip
Poruththaatrum panbe thalai.
current_meaning: The highest virtue is to show kindly regard and patiently bear with even those whose nature is to hurt us.
elementary_explanation: If a classmate keeps being mean to you, the easy thing is to be mean back. Valluvar says the very best thing is to stay kind and patient with them anyway. That is the hardest kind of kindness, and so it is the greatest.
university_explanation: ஒறுத்து ஆற்றும் பண்பினார் means ‘those whose nature is to cause harm/afflict’, and the matching பொறுத்து ஆற்றும் பண்பு is ‘the nature that bears it and carries on’; the verbal rhyme ஒறுத்து/பொறுத்து sets the injurer’s nature against the forbearer’s. கண்ணும் (‘even towards’) extends kannottam from familiar friends to enemies, the chapter’s highest reach. Commentators differ slightly on the object: Mu. Varadarasanar reads ‘even those who deserve punishment’, stressing a judge’s leniency, while Solomon Pappaiah and the English gloss read ‘those who grieve or harm us’, stressing personal forbearance; Parimelazhagar’s royal reading allows both. தலை (‘head’, i.e., foremost) ranks this above all other forms of kindness. Both texts agree; thirukkural-thamizh.org has கண்ணுங்கண் for ytamizh’s கண்ணும்கண்.

tamil:
பெயக்கண்டும் நஞ்சுண் டமைவர் நயத்தக்க
நாகரிகம் வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Peyakkandum nanjundu amaivar nayaththakka
Naagarigam vendu pavar.
current_meaning: Those who seek the courtesy that everyone admires will even drink poison they have seen poured for them by a friend, and stay at peace with that friend.
elementary_explanation: Suppose a friend gives you a cookie that tastes awful, and you know they didn’t make it right. A very gracious person might eat it and still smile, because they care more about the friend than the cookie. Valluvar tells this as an extreme story to show how far true kindness can go.
university_explanation: The couplet is deliberately hyperbolic: பெயக் கண்டும் (‘even having seen it poured’) and நஞ்சு உண்டு அமைவர் (‘they drink the poison and remain calm/content’) describe people who knowingly accept harm from someone close rather than break the bond. நாகரிகம் here does not mean modern ‘civilisation’; Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take it as the refined kannottam, the urbane courtesy that is நயத்தக்க (‘worthy of being desired’ by all). Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah specify that the poison is offered by those one has long associated with, and the Sangam anthology Natrinai (poem 355) is frequently cited for the closely related idea that the truly refined will drink even poison offered by friends. Commentators treat the couplet as illustrating the extreme limit of kannottam rather than a literal instruction. Both texts agree word for word.

tamil:
ஒற்றும் உரைசான்ற நூலும் இவையிரண்டும்
தெற்றென்க மன்னவன் கண்.
transliteration:
Otrum uraisaandra noolum ivaiyirandum
Thetrenga mannavan kan.
current_meaning: A ruler should clearly understand that he has two eyes: his spies, who show him what is actually happening, and the respected books of law, which show him what ought to be done.
elementary_explanation: A captain steering a ship needs two things: a lookout who shouts what he sees on the sea, and a map that shows the right route. With only one, the ship gets lost. This kural says a ruler is the same: he needs people who tell him what is really going on, and good rules that tell him what is right.
university_explanation: The chapter title ஒற்றாடல் means ‘the employment (ஆடல், handling) of spies’; one printed text glosses it ஒற்றரை ஆளும் திறம், ‘the skill of managing spies’. It follows directly on கண்ணோட்டம் (ch. 58, ‘the kindly eye’), and Valluvar continues the eye image by naming two organs of royal sight: ஒற்று (the spy, or intelligence generally) and உரைசான்ற நூல் (a treatise ‘full of renown’). Parimelazhagar takes the second to be the science of polity (நீதிநூல்), and the commentators draw the contrast that the treatise shows what should be done while the spy shows what is being done; a king lacking either is half-blind. The verb தெற்றென்க (‘let him know clearly’) turns the saying into a direct order. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it the same way, and the text is identical on ytamizh.com, thirukkural.net and thirukkural-thamizh.org, the last printing it in older sandhi-joined form (ஒற்று முரைசான்ற நூலு மிவையிரண்டுந்).

tamil:
எல்லார்க்கும் எல்லாம் நிகழ்பவை எஞ்ஞான்றும்
வல்லறிதல் வேந்தன் தொழில்.
transliteration:
Ellaarkkum ellaam nigazhpavai enjnjaandrum
Vallaridhal vaendhan thozhil.
current_meaning: It is a king’s job to learn quickly, at all times, everything that happens to everyone, whether enemies, friends or neutrals.
elementary_explanation: A good school principal wants to know right away if someone is being bullied, if a pipe is leaking, or if a new student feels lost, not a month later. This kural says a ruler’s real work is the same: always finding out quickly what is happening to everyone.
university_explanation: The couplet stacks three universals, எல்லார்க்கும் (to all persons), எல்லாம் (all things) and எஞ்ஞான்றும் (at all times), then adds வல் (‘swiftly’) to அறிதல் (knowing). Parimelazhagar spells out ‘all persons’ as the king’s enemies, friends and neutrals (பகைவர், நட்பினர், நொதுமலர்), and Pappaiah and Kalaignar follow this three-way division, which matches the Arthashastra’s mandala theory of foreign relations. Most commentators add ‘through spies’ in brackets because the chapter context requires it, even though the word ஒற்று is not in the line. The closing தொழில் (‘occupation, duty’) presents knowing as the king’s trade and not something he does now and then. The wording is the same on all three sources consulted; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form எல்லார்க்கு மெல்லா.

tamil:
ஒற்றினான் ஒற்றிப் பொருள்தெரியா மன்னவன்
கொற்றங் கொளக்கிடந்தது இல்.
transliteration:
Otrinaan otrip poruldheriyaa mannavan
Kotrang kolakkidandhadhu il.
current_meaning: A king who does not gather news through spies and work out what it means has no path to victory.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a football coach who never watches the other team play and never thinks about what their moves mean. He will keep losing. This kural says a leader has to find out what is going on and then think carefully about what it means.
university_explanation: The first line repeats the root ஒற்று (ஒற்றினான் ஒற்றி, ‘spying by means of a spy’), a figure of repetition that runs through the whole chapter. The key phrase is பொருள் தெரியா, ‘not discerning the meaning or import’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as not examining the benefit (பயன்) of what spies report, and Pulavar Kesikan as not working out the significance of events in enemy lands. So Valluvar is not satisfied with collecting data; the king must interpret it. The second line, கொற்றங் கொளக்கிடந்தது இல், says literally that ‘there is nothing lying there for him to take as victory’. Pappaiah widens கொற்றம் from battlefield victory to lasting success of the government. The text agrees on all three sources; thirukkural-thamizh.org prints ஒற்றினா னொற்றிப் பொருடெரியா, with the sandhi shown.

tamil:
வினைசெய்வார் தம்சுற்றம் வேண்டாதார் என்றாங்கு
அனைவரையும் ஆராய்வது ஒற்று.
transliteration:
Vinaiseyvaar thamsutram vaendaadhaar endraangu
Anaivaraiyum aaraaivadhu otru.
current_meaning: A true spy watches everyone without exception: the king’s own officials, his relatives, and his enemies alike.
elementary_explanation: A fair referee watches every player on the field, even the ones from his own town and even his friends. If he only watched one team, the game would be unfair. This kural says a good investigator checks on everyone equally.
university_explanation: Valluvar names three groups: வினைசெய்வார் (those who carry out the king’s business, i.e. officials), தம் சுற்றம் (the king’s own kin), and வேண்டாதார் (those who do not wish him well, i.e. enemies). He then sums them up in அனைவரையும் (‘all of them’). Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar take தம் to mean the king’s own relatives. Kalaignar reads the couplet as a rule of impartiality for the spy, who must not make exceptions for those he likes or dislikes. Pappaiah modernises the groups as civil servants, the ruling party, the opposition and foreigners, and says the spy reads their inner intent (மனக்கருத்து) from their words and deeds. The couplet is also a definition, ending ‘… is a spy’ (ஒற்று), a form repeated in 585-587. The text agrees across sources, with thirukkural-thamizh.org giving the sandhi form தஞ்சுற்றம்.

tamil:
கடாஅ உருவொடு கண்ணஞ்சாது யாண்டும்
உகாஅமை வல்லதே ஒற்று.
transliteration:
Kadaaa uruvodu kannanjaadhu yaandum
Ugaaamai valladhae otru.
current_meaning: A real spy has an appearance that draws no suspicion, does not flinch under anyone’s gaze, and can never be made to let out his secret anywhere.
elementary_explanation: In a game of hide-and-seek in plain sight, the best player looks totally ordinary, stays calm even when someone stares at them, and never giggles and gives themselves away. This kural says a good spy is like that: ordinary-looking, calm and able to keep a secret.
university_explanation: The couplet names three qualities, and two of its words use the lengthened vowel (அளபெடை): கடாஅ உரு, ‘a form that does not provoke questioning’ (from கடாவுதல், to interrogate), and உகாஅமை, ‘not spilling’ (from உகுத்தல், to let fall, i.e. to leak a secret). In between comes கண் அஞ்சாது, ‘not fearing the eyes’ of suspicious onlookers. Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as not fearing the looks of those who watch him. Pappaiah adds that the spy must hold out whatever method is used on him, naming the four upāyas (sāma, dāna, bheda, daṇḍa: persuasion, bribery, division, force). யாண்டும் (‘anywhere, at any time’) makes the secrecy absolute. The wording agrees across sources; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi கண்ணஞ்சா தியாண்டு முகாஅமை.

tamil:
துறந்தார் படிவத்த ராகி இறந்தாராய்ந்து
என்செயினும் சோர்விலது ஒற்று.
transliteration:
Thurandhaar padivaththa raagi irandhaaraaindhu
Enseyinum soarviladhu otru.
current_meaning: A spy takes on the guise of a renunciant, gets into places others cannot enter, investigates thoroughly, and never gives himself away, whatever is done to him.
elementary_explanation: In old stories, a clever messenger sometimes dresses as a humble traveller so he can pass through the gates. Even if guards question him roughly, he stays in character and keeps his secret. This kural describes that kind of brave, patient spy.
university_explanation: துறந்தார் படிவத்தர் ஆகி means ‘taking on the form (படிவம்) of those who have renounced’, that is, dressing as an ascetic or wandering monk. Such figures could travel freely in ancient India. இறந்து ஆராய்ந்து is read by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar as ‘going beyond [ordinary limits], into places otherwise unreachable, and examining’. Pappaiah makes it explicit: places one cannot go. என்செயினும் சோர்வு இலது means ‘whatever [the suspicious] may do to him, he does not slip’. Here சோர்வு means a lapse that gives the secret away, not tiredness, and Pappaiah and Kalaignar both read it as holding out under torture. The disguise matches the Arthashastra’s tāpasa (ascetic) spy closely, which is often cited in comparative studies of the Kural. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net give identical text; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi forms ராகி யிறந்தாராய்ந் / தென்செயினுஞ் சோர்வில தொற்று.

tamil:
மறைந்தவை கேட்கவற் றாகி அறிந்தவை
ஐயப்பாடு இல்லதே ஒற்று.
transliteration:
Maraindhavai kaetkavat raagi arindhavai
Aiyappaadu illadhae otru.
current_meaning: A spy is one who can draw out what is hidden and who is left with no doubt about what he has found.
elementary_explanation: A good detective in a mystery story does two things: she finds the hidden clues, and she checks them until she is sure before she tells anyone. Guessing isn’t enough. This kural says a real investigator uncovers secrets and makes sure they are true.
university_explanation: மறைந்தவை கேட்க வற்று ஆகி means ‘being able (வற்று, ‘capable’) to hear what is concealed’. அறிந்தவை ஐயப்பாடு இல்லது means ‘having no doubt about what has been learned’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the second half as being able to decide firmly without wavering. Pappaiah adds that the spy draws secrets ‘from the very mouth of those who did the deed’, and Kalaignar that he learns through those who are present at secret meetings. So the couplet sets two standards, access to secrets and certainty about them, and the next two couplets (588-589) add a check on that certainty from the king’s side. The text is identical across the three sources, apart from the sandhi யறிந்தவை / யையப்பா டில்லதே in thirukkural-thamizh.org.

tamil:
ஒற்றொற்றித் தந்த பொருளையும் மற்றுமோர்
ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Otrotrith thandha porulaiyum matrumoar
Otrinaal otrik kolal.
current_meaning: Even information a spy has gathered and brought in should be accepted only after it has been checked by another spy.
elementary_explanation: If one friend tells you there is no school tomorrow, you would probably check with another friend or the school website before staying home. This kural says a wise leader always double-checks a report with a second source.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on the root ஒற்று, which appears four times (ஒற்று ஒற்றித் தந்த … ஒற்றினால் ஒற்றி): ‘what a spy has spied out and delivered, have it spied out again by another spy, and then accept it’. The உம் in பொருளையும் (‘even the information’) means that even a reliable spy’s report is not exempt. Mu. Varadarasanar says it should be taken as true only after the two accounts are found to agree (ஒப்புமை கண்டபின்). Kalaignar stresses comparing the two reports before deciding. கொளல் is an infinitive-style imperative (‘one should accept’), the same form Valluvar uses for maxims elsewhere. This couplet and 589 together set out a clear doctrine of corroborating intelligence. The text agrees across all three sources.

tamil:
ஒற்றெற் றுணராமை ஆள்க உடன்மூவர்
சொற்றொக்க தேறப் படும்.
transliteration:
Otret runaraamai aalga udanmoovar
Sotrokka thaerap padum.
current_meaning: Employ spies so that none of them knows about the others; when the reports of three such spies agree, the matter can be trusted.
elementary_explanation: If three students are each asked separately what happened at recess, and they can’t talk to each other first, but all three tell the same story, the teacher can be pretty sure it is true. This kural says a wise leader checks the truth the same way.
university_explanation: The first line says to employ (ஆள்க) spies in a way that one does not become aware (உணராமை) of another. The second says that when the words of three (மூவர் சொல்) agree together (தொக்க), the thing may be trusted (தேறப்படும்). There is a real textual variant in the first word. ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print ஒற்றெற் றுணராமை, while thirukkural-thamizh.org prints ஒற்றொற் றுணராமை, i.e. ஒற்று ஒற்று உணராமை, ‘one spy not knowing another spy’. That is the sense every commentator, including Parimelazhagar, gives, and the -எற்று form is best explained as a sandhi or scribal variant. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the second line as ‘if the three agree, take it as true’. Pappaiah is more cautious: even when three agree, examine it before accepting. The rule is strikingly close to Arthashastra 1.12, which requires agreement from three independent sources and says the spy-units must not know one another.

tamil:
சிறப்பறிய ஒற்றின்கண் செய்யற்க செய்யின்
புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை.
transliteration:
Sirapariya otrinkan seyyarka seyyin
Purappaduththaan aagum marai.
current_meaning: A king should not honour a spy where others can see; if he does, he himself will have given away the secret.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a secret helper who quietly tells the teacher when someone is being picked on. If the teacher gave that helper a big prize in front of the whole class, everyone would know who the helper was, and the secret would be ruined. This kural says to thank secret helpers quietly.
university_explanation: சிறப்பு அறிய means ‘so that the honour is known [to others]’; ஒற்றின்கண் செய்யற்க, ‘do not do it to the spy’; செய்யின் புறப்படுத்தான் ஆகும் மறை, ‘if you do, you become the one who brought the secret out into the open (புறப்படுத்தல்)’. The irony is that after all the care in 585-589 to keep spies hidden, the king himself becomes the leak by rewarding them publicly. Pappaiah reads the couplet as ‘reward the spy, but reward him secretly’, which fits Sun Tzu’s and Kautilya’s view that spies must be generously paid. Mu. Varadarasanar reads மறை as both the secret information and the spy’s identity. The text agrees across sources; thirukkural-thamizh.org has the sandhi form வொற்றின்கட் செய்யற்க செய்யிற் / புறப்படுத்தா னாகு மறை.

tamil:
உடையர் எனப்படுவது ஊக்கம் அஃதில்லார்
உடையது உடையரோ மற்று.
transliteration:
Udaiyar enappaduvadhu ookkam aqdhillaar
Udaiyadhu udaiyaro matru.
current_meaning: The only thing that truly makes a person an owner is inner energy; those without it do not really possess anything, whatever else they may hold.
elementary_explanation: Imagine two children who are each given a box of paints. One gets excited and paints every day; the other leaves the box closed on a shelf. Only the first one really ‘has’ paints. The Kural says the eager, energetic spirit is the thing that makes anything you own actually yours.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by redefining possession itself: “udaiyar enappaduvadhu” (what it is to be called a possessor) is ookkam, which Parimelazhagar glosses as mental elation or upsurge of the will toward action (ullaezhuchi), the drive that animates effort rather than effort itself. The rhetorical question “udaiyadhu udaiyaro” (do they own what they own?) denies that the unenergetic possess even their existing wealth, since without ookkam it will neither be defended nor increased; “matru” is treated by the commentators as an expletive particle (asai). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all paraphrase the line as ‘only the energetic are truly possessors’, and the text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net. The adhikaram sits in Arasiyal (royalty), after Espionage and before Unsluggishness (Madiyinmai), Manly Effort (Aalvinaiyudaimai) and Not Despairing in Trouble, forming a cluster on the psychology of exertion that parallels the Sanskrit utsāha-śakti, the ‘power of energy’ that Kautilya lists among a king’s three powers. Thirukkural.net titles the chapter ‘Magnanimity’, while Pope and ytamizh.com use ‘Energy’, reflecting the double sense of ookkam as both drive and largeness of spirit.

tamil:
உள்ளம் உடைமை உடைமை பொருளுடைமை
நில்லாது நீங்கி விடும்.
transliteration:
Ullam udaimai udaimai poruludaimai
Nillaadhu neengi vidum.
current_meaning: Energy of mind is the possession that lasts; material wealth does not stay but slips away.
elementary_explanation: A sandcastle can be washed away by the next wave, but the skill and excitement that built it stay with you, so you can build another one tomorrow. Money and things can disappear, but a strong, eager mind stays yours.
university_explanation: The couplet sets two kinds of udaimai (property) against each other: ullam udaimai, possession of ‘mind’, which Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar gloss as ookkam, and porul udaimai, possession of goods. The triple repetition ‘udaimai udaimai … udaimai’ is a deliberate sound-play (sol-pin-varunilai) that forces the reader to ask which ‘having’ deserves the name. The verbs ‘nillaadhu neengi vidum’ (does not stay, departs) echo the Aram-section chapter on impermanence (Nilaiyaamai, ch. 34), but here the lesson is practical rather than renunciatory: since wealth is fugitive, the ruler’s real capital is the energy that can regain it. Solomon Pappaiah renders ullam as mana uruthi (firmness of mind), a slight shift from zeal to resolve. The text agrees verbatim in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஆக்கம் இழந்தேமென்று அல்லாவார் ஊக்கம்
ஒருவந்தம் கைத்துடை யார்.
transliteration:
Aakkam izhandhemendru allaavaar ookkam
Oruvandham kaiththudai yaar.
current_meaning: Those who firmly hold energy in their hands do not grieve, saying ‘we have lost our wealth’.
elementary_explanation: If a strong wind knocks down your block tower, you can cry about it, or you can say ‘I still have my hands and my ideas’ and build again. People with real energy don’t sit around moaning about what they lost; they know they can make more.
university_explanation: The key image is ‘kaiththu udaiyaar’: those who hold ookkam as kaipporul, ready money in the hand, which Parimelazhagar reads as the secure capital that makes lost aakkam (prosperity) recoverable. ‘Oruvandham’ means certainly or firmly (nichchayamaaga), qualifying the grip on energy; ‘allaavaar’ (will not be distressed) derives from allal, affliction. Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the implied condition ‘even when prosperity has actually been lost’, while Kalaignar stresses that such people do not lose their ookkam along with their wealth. The couplet thus answers 592: if wealth departs, energy remains the seed of its return, which is why the chapter treats ookkam as a king’s fundamental resource. The Tamil text is identical in both base sources, differing only in word-splitting (izhandhemendru vs. izhandhaem endru).

tamil:
ஆக்கம் அதர்வினாய்ச் செல்லும் அசைவிலா
ஊக்க முடையா னுழை.
transliteration:
Aakkam adharvinaaich chellum asaivilaa
Ookkam udaiyaan uzhai.
current_meaning: Prosperity itself asks the way and travels to the home of the person whose energy never wavers.
elementary_explanation: Picture good luck as a little traveller with a map, going around asking, ‘Where does the hardworking kid live?’ The Kural says success goes looking for people who never give up.
university_explanation: Valluvar personifies aakkam (prosperity, increase) as a traveller who ‘adhar vinaai’, asks the road (adhar = path), to reach the dwelling (uzhai) of the man of unwavering (asaivilaa) energy. Parimelazhagar notes that prosperity need not be sought by such a person; it seeks him, a reversal of the usual image of the striver chasing fortune. Solomon Pappaiah’s modern rendering, ‘wealth learns his address and goes to him’, keeps the playful personification. The idea closely matches the Sanskrit subhāṣita ‘udyoginaṁ puruṣa-siṁham upaiti lakṣmīḥ’ (Lakshmi approaches the lion-like man of effort), found in the Hitopadesha prologue, showing a shared Indian topos. The two base sources agree on the text; thirukkural.net joins ‘ookka mudaiyaa nuzhai’ as in the metrical manuscripts, which is simply the sandhi form of ‘ookkam udaiyaan uzhai’.

tamil:
வெள்ளத் தனைய மலர்நீட்டம் மாந்தர்தம்
உள்ளத் தனையது உயர்வு.
transliteration:
Vellath thanaiya malarneettam maandhardham
Ullath thanaiyadhu uyarvu.
current_meaning: Just as a water-flower’s stalk grows as tall as the water is deep, a person rises only as high as the energy of their mind.
elementary_explanation: A lotus in a pond always grows its stem long enough to reach the top of the water. If the pond is deep, the stem is long. The Kural says people are like that: the bigger your spirit and effort, the higher you rise.
university_explanation: This is the chapter’s most celebrated image. ‘Vellaththanaiya malar neettam’ means the length of the flower (its stalk) is proportionate to the flood or water-depth; ‘ullaththanaiyadhu uyarvu’ means human height or eminence is proportionate to ullam, which the commentators again take as ookkam. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah speak generally of neerppookkal (water-flowers), while Kalaignar specifies the lotus stalk (thaamarai thandu); the botanical observation that lotus and water-lily stems lengthen to keep the bloom at the surface underlies the comparison. The parallel structure ‘-aththanaiya … -aththanaiyadhu’ is an example of Valluvar’s use of exact grammatical symmetry (ethirnirai) to make the analogy feel like a law. The couplet implies both limit and possibility: stature cannot exceed inner energy, but greater energy raises it. Text identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உள்ளுவ தெல்லாம் உயர்வுள்ளல் மற்றது
தள்ளினுந் தள்ளாமை நீர்த்து.
transliteration:
Ulluva thellaam uyarvullal matradhu
Thallinum thallaamai neerththu.
current_meaning: Let every thought be a thought of rising higher; even if fate pushes that aim aside, it has the worth of never having been pushed aside.
elementary_explanation: If you aim to jump over a tall bar and only get halfway, you still jumped higher than if you’d aimed low. The Kural says always think big; even when you don’t reach it, the aiming itself counts.
university_explanation: The first line is a direct precept: ‘ulluvadhellaam uyarvu ullal’, let all that you think be the thinking of elevation. The second line is compressed and has produced different readings. Parimelazhagar (reflected in Pope’s ‘if it should be thrust from him by fate, it will have the nature of not being thrust from him’) takes ‘matradhu thallinum’ as ‘even if that (aim) is thwarted by fate (ool)’ and ‘thallaamai neerththu’ as ‘it has the nature (neermai) of not being thwarted’, since the nobility of the aim remains. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the line as an imperative, ‘do not abandon such thinking even if it fails’, while Solomon Pappaiah adds that the great will praise the attempt, so it counts as fulfilled. Thirukkural.net compresses this as ‘failure then is as good as success’. The text is identical in the base sources; the interpretive variation lies in whether ‘thallaamai’ is descriptive or prescriptive.

tamil:
சிதைவிடத்து ஒல்கார் உரவோர் புதையம்பிற்
பட்டுப்பா டூன்றுங் களிறு.
transliteration:
Sidhaividaththu olkaar uravor pudhaiyambir
Pattuppaadu oondrum kaliru.
current_meaning: The strong-minded do not falter even in ruin, just as a war elephant, pierced deep by arrows, stands firm and keeps its dignity.
elementary_explanation: Think of a brave firefighter who keeps going even when they are tired and hurt. The Kural compares strong-hearted people to a huge elephant that stays standing even when arrows hit it. Tough times don’t make them quit.
university_explanation: ‘Sidhaividaththu’ means at the place or time of ruin (sidhaivu), and ‘olkaar’ means they do not bend or droop; ‘uravor’ are those with uram, firmness of mind. The simile is from war: ‘pudhai ambu’ are arrows buried in the flesh, and ‘pattup paadu oondrum kaliru’ is the bull elephant that, though struck, plants itself (oondrum) and upholds its paadu, glossed by Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasanar as its perumai (greatness, dignity). The image comes from Sangam battle poetry, where the wounded tusker holding its ground is a stock emblem of valour. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads ‘pudhai’ as arrows that cover the body. The spelling ‘kaliru’ (களிறு) is the standard word for a male elephant; the texts in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree.

tamil:
உள்ளம் இலாதவர் எய்தார் உலகத்து
வள்ளியம் என்னுஞ் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Ullam ilaadhavar eydhaar ulagaththu
Valliyam ennum serukku.
current_meaning: Those who lack energy of spirit will never know the proud joy of saying, ‘We are the generous givers of the world’.
elementary_explanation: To share lots of cookies with your friends, you first have to bake them. The Kural says people without energy never get to feel the happy pride of being the one who gives to everyone, because they never make enough to give.
university_explanation: ‘Ullam ilaadhavar’ again uses ullam for ookkam; ‘vallium ennum serukku’ is the elation or proud self-regard (serukku) of being able to say ‘we are liberal’ (valliyam, from vallal, a munificent patron). The logic, drawn out by Parimelazhagar, is that liberality requires wealth, wealth requires effort, and effort requires ookkam, so the unenergetic are cut off from one of the highest satisfactions of kingship and householdership, the role of the vallal celebrated in Sangam poetry (the seven great patrons, kadaiyezhu vallalgal). Solomon Pappaiah calls it ‘mana uyarvu’, uplift of mind, while Kalaignar reads ‘ullam’ as the eager will to give freely. Sivayogi Sivakumar’s reading, ‘pride of having conquered the world’, diverges from the mainstream. Thirukkural.net’s ‘the poor in spirit can never attain the pride of being the generous patrons of the world’ matches the majority view; the Tamil is identical in both sources.

tamil:
பரியது கூர்ங்கோட்டது ஆயினும் யானை
வெரூஉம் புலிதாக் குறின்.
transliteration:
Pariyadhu koorngottadhu aayinum yaanai
Veruum pulidhaakkurin.
current_meaning: Though the elephant is huge and armed with sharp tusks, it takes fright when a tiger attacks.
elementary_explanation: A big dog can run away from a small, brave cat that hisses and charges. The Kural says size and weapons don’t decide who wins; the fierce spirit does, like a tiger that can scare an elephant.
university_explanation: The couplet is a pure illustration (eduththukkaattu uvamai) with the moral left implicit: ‘pariyadhu’ (bulky) and ‘koorng kottadhu’ (having sharp tusks) list the elephant’s physical advantages, and ‘veruum’ (fears) is an alapedai (vowel-lengthened) form of verum, which heightens the sense of sudden fright. Parimelazhagar explains that the tiger prevails because it has ookkam, and that the verse teaches that energy, not bulk or weaponry, decides contests; Kalaignar makes this explicit, calling ookkam stronger than physique. The pairing with 597, where the elephant is the image of steadfastness, shows Valluvar using the same animal both ways: wounded but energetic it stands, huge but unenergetic it flees. The text is identical in the base sources; transliterations differ only in rendering the alapedai (veru-um / veruum).

tamil:
உரமொருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கைஅஃ தில்லார்
மரம்மக்க ளாதலே வேறு.
transliteration:
Uram oruvarku ulla verukkai aqdhillaar
Maram makkal aadhale veru.
current_meaning: A person’s real strength is abundance of inner energy; those without it are trees, differing from them only in having human shape.
elementary_explanation: A tree stands in one place all day and never tries anything new. The Kural says a person with no energy or drive is like a tree that happens to look like a human. What makes us truly alive is our eagerness to act.
university_explanation: ‘Uram’ is strength or firmness, and ‘ulla verukkai’ is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar takes verukkai as abundance, hence ‘excess of ookkam is one’s strength’, while others take verukkai in its lexical sense of wealth (selvam), hence ‘energy is the mind’s wealth’, which is Pope’s ‘energy is mental wealth’. Solomon Pappaiah glosses uram as thinniya arivu (firm understanding). The second line’s ‘maram makkal aadhale veru’ is devastating: the only difference (veru) between the energy-less and trees is that they have become human in form. Parimelazhagar notes the chapter closes by returning to 591, where the energy-less were denied possession; here they are denied full humanity. The text is identical in the base sources; the sandhi form ‘verukkaiaqdhillaar’ contains the aaydham (ஃ) of ‘aqdhu’.
